title: Converting between effect sizes
text:
Many effect sizes can be inter-converted (Borenstein et al. 2021, Lajeunesse 2026) These conversions make assumptions and can bias the resulting effect types (see (Poom and Wåhlberg 2022)) and should be carefully used—with sensitivity analyses to ensure that the conversions aren’t unduly influencing results.
At the same time, especially for questions with limited data, we believe that conversions are an important tool in the meta-analyst toolkit.


Effect size types


Converting effect sizes requires several assumptions. We summarize these in the table below:






Conversion
Assumption



lnOR ↔︎ SMD
Response variable is a discretized version of an underlying continuous variable


SMD ↔︎ Zr
Predictor variable is a discretized version of an underlying continuous variable


lnOR ↔︎ Zr
Response and predictor have an underlying continuous reality


SMD ↔︎ lnRoM
Homogeneity of variances between groups









Warning



What about comparing truly discrete to continuous? Are there any cases where this is desired or needed? Perhaps in behavioral data?
Because \(r_{pb}\) (point biserial correlation) is for naturally discrete groups and this can be calculated from means±sd and then you can convert to Zr (though Jacobs and Viechtbauer (2017) say you shouldn’t? because sampling variance isn’t correct? though it’s probably ok to do).
READ Jacobs and Viechtbauer (2017)



In addition to these assumptions, be careful that the data is truly comparable, especially in terms of their units of replication—otherwise the converted effect size will have vastly higher or lower weights in the final meta-analytic model.
For example, imagine you’re analyzing the effect of an introduced predator on prey abundance. Some studies present abundance correlations of the predator and prey (Zr), where the unit of replication is the number of surveys. Other studies report the presence and absence of prey species on islands with and without the predator (lnOR), for which the unit of replication is number of islands (each of which was presumably surveyed many times).
Both of these study types are relevant to the same question–—the effect of the predator on prey abundance. Likewise, converting betwee these effect sizes does not violate the assumptions in the table above because presence-absence is a discretized version of abundance. It is thus possible to convert these effect sizes via SMD to include both papers in the same model.
However, the units of replication of these study types are vastly different (study 1 = survey; study 2 = island). This means the Zr abundance correlations will have more weight than the full-island lnOR responses.
However, in many other cases, conversions will allow similar data to be compared without comparing different units of replication.
Given the assumptions and potential biases involved in converting effect sizes, we recommend that you convert minority effect sizes to the dominant effect size in your dataset after confirming that assumptions are met and that the unit of replication for all the effect sizes are equivalent. We then recommend running your models with and without these converted effect sizes, to evaluate whether the inclusion of minority effect sizes alter your results.






ImportantAlternative to conversion: reconstruct the underlying data



In some cases, converting between effect sizes can be prevented by reconstructing the underlying data of the author-presented summaries and summarizing these data into the desired analysis effect size, which can align the units of replication between studies.
See examples for SMD-type effect sizes, lnOR effect sizes, Zr effect sizes, and for non-Gaussian responses



We have digitized the primary conversion formulas and they are available in our convert_effect_sizes() function. Running the function on its own will return a table with the statistics required for each conversion.

convert_effect_sizes()


Effect type name must be specified with 'effect_type' argument
    and provide necessary variables (as named arguments, e.g., n1 = group1_n or a numeric vector).
 
Returning effect size names & required variables for reference.


   from_effect to_effect  vars_required
        <char>    <char>         <char>
1:        lnOR       SMD yi, vi, n1, n2
2:          Zr       SMD      yi, vi, n
3:           r       SMD           r, n
4:         SMD        Zr yi, vi, n1, n2
5:         SMD      lnOR yi, vi, n1, n2
6:       lnRoM       SMD yi, vi, n1, n2
7:          Zr      lnOR      yi, vi, n
8:        lnOR        Zr     yi, n1, n2


To convert an effect size, specify the from effect type and the to effect type, as well as the required statistics. Note that this function also supports full, two-step conversions from Zr to lnOR and vice versa.
We’ll now show the math and demonstrate the conversions in R. SMD is the universal solvent of these conversions and it is important to remember that SMD has multiple estimators. The most commonly used is Hedges’ \(g\), which has a small sample size bias correction factor \(J\). However, all conversion formulas convert to and from \(d\), an alternative estimator of SMD that lacks this correction factor. For that reason, the math below will skip this conversion and be written for \(d\) instead of \(g\) based on this conversion.
\[
\begin{aligned}
&J = 1-\frac{3}{4*(n_1 + n_2 - 2) - 1}\\
&d = \frac{m1-m2}{sd_{pooled}}\\
&d = \frac{g}{J}
\end{aligned}
\] Note that the default sampling variance estimator for Hedges’ g is the same estimator used for Cohen’s d (in the R package escalc. Thus no conversion from Var(d) to Var(g) is necessary.






ImportantAlternative estimators and effect size conversion



As described earlier in this tutorial, there are multiple flavors of estimators for many effect sizes including paired estimators and, for SMD, an estimator that tolerates heteroscedastic data (“SMDH”). To the best of our knowledge, there are no conversion formulas for these alterative estimators.
This means that if you are converting Zr effect sizes to add to a meta-analysis that is otherwise composed of SMD-type effect sizes, you won’t be able to use SMDH for the larger dataset. Conversely, if you have paired SMD-type data that you wish to convert to add to a meta-analysis of Zr effect sizes, you’ll have to ignore the paired design.

title: Converting between effect sizes
text:
SMD → lnOR
This conversion assumes that the response variable is continuous (e.g., undergirding the binary response of the lnOR effect type) and that it has a logistic distribution (similar to a normal distribution).
If the lnOR data was presence/absence of a species and the SMD data was abundance, we believe this assumption is satisfied, given that presence/absence are the extreme ends of abundance.
Let \(yi_{lnOR}\) and \(yi_{d}\) be the point estimate for the lnOR and Cohen’s d effect sizes and \(vi_{lnOR}\) and \(vi_{d}\) be their sampling variances:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&yi_{lnOR} = yi_d * \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{3}} \\
&vi_{lnOR} = vi_{d} * \frac{\pi^2}{3} \\
\end{aligned}
\]
In R:

convert_effect_sizes(from = "SMD",
                     to = "lnOR",
                     yi = 0.9,
                     vi = 0.01,
                     n1 = 15,
                     n2 = 15)

This conversion assumes that the continuous data has a logistic distribution. 
Please use conversions carefully and conduct sensitivity analyses. 
Note that the 'vi' is assumed to have been calculated with `metafor::escalc` package defaults (variance of 'd' not 'g')

title: Converting between effect sizes
text:
SMD → Zr
This conversion assumes that a continuous variable was discretized to form the treatment and control groups of an SMD effect size. This may be the case in some situations (e.g., if treatment and control were based on the presence or absence of an independent variable treatment while the correlation was across a continuous gradient of the same variable).
To convert from SMD to Zr, we first convert \(d\) to the correlation coefficient \(r\) and then to Zr, using a correction factor \(a\) for cases where \(n_1 \neq n_2\). Let \(yi_{Zr}\) and \(yi_d\) be the point estimate for Zr and Cohen’s d:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&a = \frac{(n_1 + n_2)^2}{n_1*n_2} \\
&r = \frac{yi_d}{\sqrt{yi_d^2 + a}} \\
&r \leftarrow \min(1, \max(-1, r_i))\\
&yi_{Zr} = atanh(r)\\
\end{aligned}
\]
And the sampling variance of Zr (\(vi_{Zr}\)): \[
\begin{aligned}
&n = n1 + n2 \\
&vi_{Zr} = \frac{1}{(n - 3)} \\
\end{aligned}
\]
In R:

convert_effect_sizes(from = "SMD",
                     to = "Zr",
                     yi = 0.9,
                     vi = 0.01,
                     n1 = 15,
                     n2 = 15)

This conversion assumes a continuous variable was dichotomized to create the treatment and control groups. 
Note that the 'vi' is assumed to have been calculated with 'metafor::escalc' defaults (variance of 'd' not 'g'). 
Like usual, be careful :) 


    yi_trans   vi_trans
       <num>      <num>
1: 0.4474395 0.03703704

This can be done in escalc directly with the measure “ZBIS”, which calculates teh biserial correlation coefficient and converts it to Zr.

escalc(measure = "ZBIS",
       m1i = 10, m2i = 7,

However, Jacobs and Viechtbauer (2017) advised against comparing this to correlation coefficients calculated from 2 continuous variables (\(r\)) or from one artificially discretized variable (\(r_b\)).

title: Converting between effect sizes
text:
Zr → SMD
First, convert the point estimate of Zr (\(yi_{Zr}\)) to the correlation coefficient \(r\) and calculate the variance of \(r\) (\(vi_r\)): \[
\begin{aligned}
&r = tanh(yi_{Zr}) \\
&vi_r = \frac{(1-r^2)^2}{(n-1)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Then calculate the point estimate (\(yi_d\)) and variance (\(vi_d\)) of Cohen’s d:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&yi_d = \frac{2*r}{\sqrt{1-r^2}} \\
&vi_d = \frac{4*vi_r}{(1-r^2)^3} \\
\end{aligned}
\]
In R:

convert_effect_sizes(from = "Zr",
                     to = "SMD",
                     yi = 0.9,
                     vi = 0.01,
                     n = 50)

'yi' is assumed to be 'Zr' (r-to-z transformed correlation coefficient). 
It may be preferable to supply 'r' and 'n' instead. To do so specify 'r' in the 'from' argument and provide a vector of correlation coefficients named 'r'. 
This conversion assumes that the underlying data was continuous with a bivariate normal distribution, with the two groups created by dichotomozing one of the two variables.

title: Discrete outcomes between two groups
text:
The log odds ratio (lnOR) and risk ratio (lnRR) effect sizes are based on two-group contingency tables. These study designs use a discrete treatment and have a discrete binary outcome. Are they dead or alive, did they breed or not, etc. Such data looks like this, where a, b, c, d are integer count values.
These outcomes are binomial, i.e., are discrete processes with binary outcomes that occur to individuals. Individuals can be both individual organisms as well as individual sites/islands/plots, i.e., in terms of presence or absence of some binary condition.
Tertiary outcomes binomial outcomes are also possible and need to be handled with alternative effect sizes. For example, the frequency of alleles (AA, Aa, aa) in a population can be described with the Hardy-Weinburg Equilibrium effect size (Wellek et al. 2010). These are not discussed in this tutorial.

The log odds ratio is the ratio of two odds:

&lnOR = log(\frac{a * d}{b * c}) \\
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}\]

title: Discrete outcomes between two groups
text:
log Risk Ratio (lnRR)
The risk ratio (or relative risk, lnRR) is similar to lnOR. While lnOR describes the odds of an event occurring, lnRR measures the probability of an event happening in one group relative to the others. The log risk ratio may be more easy to interpret but has numeric properties that make lnOR statistically preferable in many cases (Borenstein et al. 2021).
lnRR is defined as:
\[\begin{aligned}
&p1 = a/n1 \\
&p2 = c/n2 \\
&lnRR = log(p1/p2) \\
\end{aligned} \tag{3}\]
Assumptions
KYLE
Interpretation
To interpret lnRR, we will also exponentiate it to convert it from log scale:

out <- escalc(measure = "RR",
       ai = 35, bi = 12,
       ci = 15, di = 21)

exp(out$yi[1])

[1] 1.787234


A risk ratio of 1.79 indicates that the probability of survival in the drug group is 1.79 times the probability of survival in the placebo group. This follows the table and code above, where the event in the first column is survival.

title: Discrete outcomes between two groups
text:
Continuity corrections
lnOR breaks down whenever \(a\), \(b\), \(c\), or \(d\) equal 0. To overcome this, we apply a continuity correction (Yates 1934) by adding 0.5 to all cells if any cell equals 0.
lnRR breaks down when \(a\) or \(c\) equal 0 and thus also requires a continuity correction. For lnRR, you add 0.5 to the affected group (not both groups) and add 1 to n1 or n2, respectively.
These continuity corrections are applied by escalc by default.

title: Universal extraction challenges
text: There are a suite of challenges, regardless of effect size type, that challenge accurate and robust meta-analysis. We’ll discuss some of them here. Note that many of our examples pertain especially to the ecology and evolution literature yet we suspect they are pervasive and widespread.

title: Universal extraction challenges
text:
Unit of replication
The unit of replication are the replicates across which summaries were calculated. In the example above, the number of surveys, or camera trap nights, or kilometers driven. With lnOR and lnRR type effect sizes, the unit of replication is generally straightforward: the number of individuals, plots, or sites across which a discrete outcome was measured.
In correlational effect sizes (Zr), the unit of replication is usually the number of measurements, unless the data presents data summarized into means±sd per value of a continuous predictor variable (see here for how to resolve these).
In SMD-type effect sizes, the unit of replication will be whatever are summarized into a central tendency and measurement of error. SMD-type effect sizes are often straightforward with behavioral or physiological data—where the unit of replication is generally the number of individuals.
However, survey or plot data adds increasing complexity. For example, if you are meta-analyzing vegetation data you may find studies that make their plots the unit of replication (pooling data from subplots) while others make subplots the unit of replication. Nested data structures like this can also occur from multiple tissue measurements nested within individuals or from egg measurements nested within nests. These are the types of non-independence structures that mixed effect models are built to handle yet these non-independence structures are often ignored in meta-analysis.
For these reasons, we recommend recording the unit of replication (e.g., individual, plot, subplot, survey) in your dataset. This information can be used for sensitivity analyses and subgroup analyses.






ImportantUnit of replication mismatches



You will likely find that different studies in your meta-analytic dataset use different units of replication to answer the same question. If your dataset is large, this heterogeneity is likely of little importance. However, if your dataset is small, these differences in unit of replication are liable to bias your model estimates.
For example, if authors provide \(mean±sd\) of survivorship of individuals across sites, the unit of replication for the raw mean±sd is number of sites. However, imagine other studies in your dataset report data for which the unit of replication is individuals. The studies that report unit of replication at the individual level will likely have much higher sample size than the study that reports data at the site level—and will thus have more influence in your models, even if they ultimately were more comprehensive and thorough in their research.
There are dark magic techniques—with their own assumptions and risks—for reconstructing the underlying data in these cases. These techniques involve drawing simulated data from the original data generating process. See examples for SMD-type effect sizes, lnOR effect sizes, Zr effect sizes, and for non-Gaussian responses.








NoteRandom effect meta-analytic models reduce the influence of sampling variance



In a common-effects meta-analytic model (which we don’t recommend in ecology and evolution), an effect size’s weight is one over its sampling variance. In the random-effects and multilevel models you will actually fit, weight is one over the sampling variance plus the between-study variance \(\tau^2\). That extra term acts as a floor on everyone’s uncertainty and compresses the differences between studies considerably: with a moderate \(\tau^2\) of \(0.1\), a twentyfold gap in sampling variance shrinks to roughly fivefold. Large studies still dominate, but far less than the raw sample sizes suggest.

title: Universal extraction challenges
text:
Measurement scale
Another issue that haunts some meta-analyses—at least in ecology—is plot size (Spake et al. 2021). For an equal effort, studies with larger plots (e.g., 100 m2) will have a smaller sample size than studies with small plots (e.g., 10 m2). Likewise, some studies will not use areal plots at all but will instead use transects (e.g., of 100 m in length).
These differences in scale are also ecological. Many if not all ecological processes are scale dependent: a negative relationship at plot scales can translate to a positive relationship at landscape scales. Likewise, a process that reduces heterogeneity at local scales can increase heterogeneity at broader scales (Wiens 1989, Ferraro and Lienau 2025).
There is currently no statistical solution for these scale challenges in meta-analysis (Spake et al. 2021). For that reason, we recommend digitizing plot-size when conducting a meta-analysis on vegetation or other scale-variable data, which can be used as a moderator or for subsetting your dataset. You’ll also notice, if thinking about this problem, that measurement scale does not operate alone but in interaction with the size of the organisms in question: a 100 m2 plot in a grassland is very different than a 100 m2 plot in an old growth forest.
Given that scale is both biologically and statistically profound, we suggest that digitizing measurement scale for explicit analysis would be worthwhile (though it is rarely done). Note that doing so is not always fruitful (e.g., (Lundgren et al. 2024)), perhaps because it is difficult to account for plant size.






NoteRemote sensing analyses



One issue that we do not know how to deal with are estimates made from remote sensing data, which is increasingly relevant in ecology as space-based data become more common-place. However, what is the sample size in a pixel-based analysis? The number of pixels? If so, then the sample size could be in the millions. Likewise, given their spatial non-independence, these pixels are not true replicates.
Finally, remote sensing analyses generally derive from publicly available data products, that form the basis for multiple studies—adding another level of non-independence that may be absent from the rest of your meta-analytic dataset.
For these reasons, we are not sure remote sensing based analyses should be meta-analyzed—or at least we don’t think they should be lumped with effect sizes generated from field data.

title: Universal extraction challenges
text:
Repeated measurements
Time series random effects are fairly straightforward to implement in the primary frequentist package for meta-analytic models (metafor and rma.mv, Viechtbauer (2010)). Controlling for them requires creating a time series column with a simple numeric value that describes temporal ordering of measurements (e.g., 1, 2, 3, 4). An additional column should provide a grouping variable.
To illustrate, let’s imagine we are assessing the influence of temperature on the growth rates of clams. A study reports an experimental trial for two species (zebra mussels and quagga mussels), each through time. The control is ambient conditions while the treatment is elevated temperature.

Now, to demonstrate how we’d control for these non-independence structures, let’s calculate an effect size (SMD) and run a model. Note we have complex non-independence structures here. One of the same species shows up in both studies (so becomes a crossed random effect), we have time sequences nested within an experiment id, and we have a shared control id.






Note



Crossed and nested random effects are confusing. Nested random effects occur when the inner level is unique to the outer level. For example, an independent experiment within an article Crossed random effects happen when a random effect level occurs across other random effect levels. For example, the same species studied across multiple articles.


Ultimately, we would also likely want to add a phylogenetic dissimilarity matrix to control for phylogenetic distance between the species. And perhaps (at least in a field study), we should also control for spatial non-independence between studies. But let’s leave that out for now. See Mizuno et al. (2026) for a tutorial on phylogenetic and spatial meta-analytic models and see Nakagawa et al. (2023) for further discussion on controlling for non-independence in meta-analysis.

library("metafor")

# First calculate effect size:
full_dat <- escalc(measure = "SMD",
                   m1i = mean_low, m2i = mean_high,
                   sd1i = sd_low, sd2i = sd_high,
                   n1i = n_low, n2i = n_high, 
                   data = full_dat) |> setDT()

# Calculate difference in temperature to use as a moderator:
full_dat[, temperature_diff := as.numeric(gsub("ºC", "", temperature_high)) - as.numeric(gsub("ºC", "", temperature_low))]

# Add a unique ID for each effect size:
full_dat[, effect_size_id := 1:.N]

# Model
m <- rma.mv(yi ~ temperature_diff,
            V = vi,
            random = list(~1 | article_id / control_id / effect_size_id,
                          ~1 | species,
                          ~time_sequence | experiment_id),
            dfs = "contain",
            test = "t",
            method = "REML",
            struct = "AR",
            data = full_dat)

To evaluate model overfitting, you can look for \(\sigma^2\) values that approach 0. \(\sigma^2\) describe the variation explained by each random effect level. In rma.mv, the model summary reports \(\sigma^2\) as sigma2 and it be accessed in the model object as follows:

            V = vi,
            random = list(~1 | article_id / control_id / effect_size_id,
                          ~1 | species,
                          ~time_sequence | experiment_id),
            dfs = "contain",
            test = "t",
            method = "REML",
            struct = "AR",
            data = full_dat)

m$sigma2

We recommend constructing a series of random effect structures, from complex to simple, running all the models, screening out \(\sigma^2 \approx 0\), and selecting the best model with AIC or AICc. See XXXX for a tutorial on model selection and overfitting in meta-analysis.






ImportantEffect size choices to reduce nuisance heterogeneity



In the example above, we are forced to use the difference in temperature as a moderator. However, alternatively, we could have calculated Zr, after drawing the underlying data for each temperature treatment with the mean, standard deviation, and sample size. We demonstrate this here.
Another option would be to calculate single-group effect sizes for each temperature treatment, and to use the temperature directly in our models (instead of the difference in temperature). There are a variety of single-group effect sizes, which we describe in the appendix for this (and other) purposes.
Finally, a third option would have been to use a totally different (and more unusual effect size): Q10. This effect size would have allowed us to capture the temperature difference explicitly, thus yielding simpler models and (potentially) less heterogeneity. We discuss this further here.
For more discussion of how to accomodate experimental designs (so called nuisance heterogeneity) explicitly into your effect size calculations, instead of into your models see Noble et al. (2022).

title: Effect sizes in meta-analysis
text:
Introduction
Meta-analysis has grown to be one of the powerful methods in science. By extracting data from across the literature, a meta-analyst can answer age-old questions at scales previously unimaginable. Moreover, meta-analysis can test for and correct publication bias and can thus not only control for biases in the literature base but provide a bridge between empirical questions (i.e., what is) and metascientific questions (e.g., how scientists construct knowledge).
Meta-analysis can be really hard. Meta-analytic methods continue to proliferate, with new effect sizes, models, and methods being published constantly. The literature has become a minefield of articles and tutorials of ‘best practices’ that can be bewildering for even the most experienced meta-analyst to keep up with.
We here present a living tutorial to navigating this methodological tempest, with particular emphasis on understanding effect sizes and extracting them from a variety of data formats. This tutorial is maintained by the Collaboration for Open Science and Synthesis in Ecology and Evolution at the University of Alberta, which is led by Professor Shinichi Nakagawa—one of the principle developers of new meta-analytic methods. While many of the examples in this tutorial derive from our experiences in ecology and evolution, which is rife with messy data, we believe the contents are applicable broadly.
We hope that this tutorial, by integrating tips and tricks and statistical know-how from across the decades and into the future, can increase the consistency, reliability, and reproducibility of meta-analytic research.
Should we add more of an overview of what meta-analysis is?


How to use this tutorial
We begin by discussing the dominant effect size types, their numeric assumptions, and how to interpret them. We then discuss the nuts and bolts of planning data extraction.
We then go into detail about universal challenges in extracting and calculating effect sizes and present effect-size specific pages about how to deal with the many odd and unusual data formats that you may uncover.
We conclude with a discussion of how to convert between effect size types. Finally, we also present some additional helpful material, including descriptions of effect sizes that estimate differences in variability and magnitude between groups and effect sizes for single group descriptive statistics. These effect size types are also summarized in a cheatsheet for the many options available in metafor’s escalc function (Viechtbauer 2010)—the workhorse of effect size calculation and meta-analysis.
This tutorial is based on an R workflow and assumes that the users have a basic understanding of R. This tutorial is viewable as a webpage or you can clone the repo and run the .qmd files interactively.


Voyaging among the ghosts of data past
Meta-analyses are powerful. But they are full of tedium. And dealing with the challenges that we describe in this tutorial (hopefully in plain english) can be overwhelming.
Yet there is something beautiful and very human about doing a meta-analysis. You encounter the heartwork and hardwork of dozens or hundreds or thousands of fellow human beings. Stories from last year or 50 years ago, from people exploring, observing, experimenting, and trying to understand our universe.
These voyagers left us breadcrumbs. Sometimes as simple as a mean and a standard deviation. Sometimes as complex as some strange contour plot drawn on a piece of graph paper and scanned in 1975. Extracting their data summaries (or finding their raw datasets) brings their work to life and allows us to continue their quests.
While you struggle to deal with all the strange and bizarre and difficult and annoying decisions these voyagers sometimes made to communicate their tales, remember to feel compassion and awe for the work that came before us–these efforts to describe the mysteries of our world.


A living tutorial
This tutorial is a living document. As such, please help us keep it alive and useful. If we missed anything, if we made an error, or overlooked an extraction challenge, please file an Issue on our github page here.







References

Viechtbauer, W. 2010. Conducting meta-analyses in R with the metafor package. Journal of Statistical Software 36:1–48.

title: Continuous predictors
text:
Zr is the dominant effect size for describing correlations. In particular, cases with a continuous predictor variable and one or two continuous response variables. Zr takes the correlation coefficient (\(r\)) and sample size as its inputs. The point estimate itself is the arc-tangent of the correlation coefficient (which must be bounded between -1 and 1).
\[\begin{aligned}
&r_{i} \leftarrow \min(1, \max(-1, r_i))\\
&Z_{r_i} = atanh(r_{i})\\
\end{aligned} \tag{1}\]
The sampling variance of Zr depends entirely on sample size and is defined as:
\[\begin{aligned}
&Var(Z_r) = \frac{1}{n-3} \\
\end{aligned} \tag{2}\]
As you can see, sampling variance is only calculable if \(n>3\).
In escalc, this looks like:
escalc(ri = 0.7, ni = 15,
       measure = "ZCOR")


      yi     vi 
1 0.8673 0.0833
Zr has among the least biased of point estimate and variance formulas (REF).

Other correlation types
Point-biserial correlations & biserial correlations
Point-biserial and biserial correlations are oddballs. They are very similar to SMD, in that they are an effect size that summarizes the relationship between a discrete predictor and a continuous outcome variable. However, these effect sizes are a measure of association/correlation and range from -1 to 1, instead of describing the difference in magnitude and direction.
Point-biserial correlations are for truly distinct predictor variables (e.g., male vs female) while biserial correlations are for continuous variables that have been turned into discrete variables (e.g., large versus small or presence versus absence).
Shouldn’t use male vs female as example of truly discrete variables
According to @Jacobs2017-cv, you should not convert point-biserial correlations to correlation coefficients. However, you can convert biserial correlations. escalc provides a shorthand to directly convert these statistics to Zr

# For the biserial correlation coefficient (for a continuous predictor that was discretized), directly to `Zr`
escalc(measure = "ZBIS",
      m1i = 13.5, m2i = 10.1,
      sd1i = 1.5, sd2i = 2.1,
      n1i = 15, n2i = 15)


      yi     vi 
1 1.3330 0.1467 


In our mind, the biggest advantage of calculating biserial correlations is that they require fewer assumptions to convert to Zr. For example, if you are doing a meta-analysis where the majority of your data are correlations except for one or two studies that use discrete predictors, it may be better to calculate biserial correlations for these studies instead of calculating SMD and then converting SMD to Zr.

title: Variability between groups
text:
PASTED TOGETHER CONTENT FROM SEPARATE PAGES. NOT EDITED
The most commonly used effect sizes concern mean relationships. However, variability is itself a meaningful dimension of reality, not merely noise. In ecological contexts, heterogeneity is considered a key driver of biodiversity and ecosystem functioning (Stein et al. 2014, Levine et al. 2016). Likewise, in evolution, variability tells us important information about selective pressures which can either act to increase variation (Buckley and Huey 2016, O’Dea et al. 2016) or reduce variation (Crispo 2007).
There are two main effect sizes for calculating variability or heteroscedasticity between two groups (i.e., discrete predictors): lnVR and lnCVR (Nakagawa et al. 2015).

title: Variability between groups
text:
lnVR
\[
\mathrm{lnVR}=\ln\left(\frac{sd_1}{sd_2}\right),
\tag{1}\]
where \(sd_1\) is the treatment-group standard deviation and \(sd_2\) is the control-group standard deviation. With the direction used throughout this chapter:

\(\mathrm{lnVR}>0\): the treatment group is more variable;
\(\mathrm{lnVR}=0\): the groups have equal standard deviations;
\(\mathrm{lnVR}<0\): the treatment group is less variable.

For the plant-biomass example:
\[
\mathrm{lnVR}=\ln\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)\approx0.405.
\]
Back-transforming gives \(e^{0.405}\approx1.5\), so the standard deviation is approximately 50% higher under warming. The lnRoM and lnVR analyses together provide a more complete biological description: warming increased mean biomass by 20% and was also associated with greater variation among plants.
Calculate lnVR as a separate outcome rather than combining lnRoM and lnVR values in one univariate model:

escalc(measure = "VR",
       sd1i = 3, n1i = 20,
       sd2i = 2, n2i = 20)


      yi     vi 
1 0.4055 0.0526 


Interpret the two analyses separately. They address related but distinct questions: lnRoM concerns proportional differences in means, whereas lnVR concerns ratios of standard deviations.






WarningUse lnCVR carefully: its value depends directly on the means



The log coefficient of variation ratio (lnCVR) compares standard deviations after dividing each one by its group mean (Nakagawa et al. 2015):
\[
\mathrm{lnCVR}
=\ln\left(\frac{s_1/m_1}{s_2/m_2}\right)
=\mathrm{lnVR}-\mathrm{lnRoM},
\tag{2}\]
before any small-sample bias corrections. Because the means occur directly in this formula, a change in lnCVR can arise from a change in the standard deviations, a change in the means, or both.
lnCVR is intended to account for a common biological pattern: groups with larger means often also have larger variances. However, dividing by the mean makes an implicit scaling assumption. In simple terms, it works most naturally when the standard deviation increases roughly in proportion to the mean. Equivalently, variance then increases roughly with the square of the mean.
That relationship differs among data types:

Approximately normal data with constant variance: the standard deviation may stay similar as the mean changes. The coefficient of variation will then change mechanically with the mean.
Poisson count data: variance equals the mean, so standard deviation increases with the square root of the mean rather than directly with the mean. The coefficient of variation therefore decreases as the mean increases.
Negative-binomial count data: variance can increase much faster than the mean. At large means, the standard deviation may be close to proportional to the mean, but the relationship depends on the dispersion parameter.
Proportions and other bounded responses: variance is constrained by the mean and commonly shrinks near the boundaries. The mean–variance relationship can therefore be strong and nonlinear.

For these reasons, do not choose lnCVR automatically. First plot or model the relationship between group means and standard deviations across the dataset. Use lnCVR when relative variability is the intended estimand and its assumed mean–variance scaling is plausible. Otherwise, report lnVR alongside lnRoM, examine the mean–variance relationship directly, or consider an arm-based model of means and standard deviations.


lnVR
lnVR is the log-transformed variability ratio, defined as \(log(\frac{sd_1}{sd_2})\). This effect size is not standardized by the mean. For that reason, this effect size can be applied to measurements derived from groups with a mean ≤ 0. However, the means need to be directly comparable.
This can be calculated in escalc with the measure = “VR”.

escalc(measure = "VR",
       sd1i = 1.5, sd2i = 2.5,
       n1i = 15, n2i = 15)

There is a paired version of lnVR as well, which requires an estimate of the correlation between group 1 and 2, which we can specify as 0.5 or 0.8 if it’s unreported (which is typical, see here):
In escalc this is specified with the “VRC” measure:

escalc(measure = "VRC",
       sd1i = 1.5, sd2i = 2.5,
       ni = 15, ri = 0.5)

lnCVR
lnCVR is the log-transformed coefficient of variation ratio, defined as \(log(\frac{sd_1/m_1}{sd_2/m_2})\). This effect size is standardized by the mean allowing you to compare groups with different means. SO THIS ISN”T TRUE?!
However, this effect size cannot accept negative values in the mean, requiring positive, ratio-scale data like the lnRoM effect size.
This can be calculated in escalc with the measure = “CVR”. This effect size requires the same statistical ingredients as SMD and lnRoM:

escalc(measure = "CVR",
       m1i = 15, m2i = 15,
       sd1i = 1.5, sd2i = 2.5,
       n1i = 15, n2i = 15)

There is a paired version of lnCVR as well. In escalc this is specified with the “CVRC” measure:

escalc(measure = "CVRC",
        m1i = 15, m2i = 15,
       sd1i = 1.5, sd2i = 2.5,
       ni = 15, ri = 0.5)

Zr describes correlations or relationships with a continuous predictor variable (and generally a continuous response variable). Zr is thus an important effect size in the meta-analyst tool kit, especially with observational data.
Zr type data often takes the form of a scatterplot but other formats exist (e.g., matrices, time series, and model estimates). We’ll go through these examples in turn, along with solutions and limitations for extracting Zr type data. We’ll start, however, by describing how to structure a database for Zr type effect sizes.

In general, Zr effect size extractions require a long-format database for data entry, where each row is one of the points in the corresponding analysis. This dataset is then summarized in R to derive \(r\) (the correlation coefficient from cor.test) and sample size (\(n\)) and a single row per unique correlation. What if there is an ugly cluster of overlapping points?








If the total number of points is reported for the study, you can duplicate the values of the red points as many times as it takes to match the total sample size. Otherwise, you’ll just have to digitize as many as you can and use a sample size that may be less than the real sample size (which makes the overall Zr estimate more conservative—e.g., less weight in the model).

title: Continuous predictor
text:
Single axis error bars
But what do you do if each point is actually a mean±SD?








If the error bars are only on the y axis this is fairly straightforward but is a bit surprising. In this case, each point actually has an internal sample size, which will need to be gleaned from the methods of the paper. After determining this internal sample size, you can extract the means and SDs for each point and then draw a random sample of the data underlying each point from the appropriate statistical distribution (with the length of this sample equal to the internal sample size).
One of the biggest reasons to draw the underlying data from figures like this is to align the units of replication between these data and the rest of your dataset. For example, if the rest of your dataset uses individuals (or nests or plots) as the unit of replication but the figure above uses sites and reports the mean±sd across individuals, then you will have a serious mismatch in the units of replication between these effect sizes. This mismatch will underweight the above effect size in your models.
Here we’ll demonstrate using rnorm to draw normally distributed data for each point. Note that it is also possible to draw data from other distributions (see here and here for a worked example with a Zr-type effect size and the binomial distribution)

Simulating underlying data, as in the example above, can help align the units of replication of your dataset.
However, one should be thoughtful and careful about the non-independence structures embedded within these summaries. The resulting effect size may be based on a mixture of more and less independent data. For example, in the correlation plots above, there are two types of non-independence: the measurements across the x-axis locations and the summarized measurements within each mean±sd.
Reconstructing the underlying data with rnorm, as we demonstrated above, and then summarizing by the mean±sd of each treatment group may mix these non-independence structures.
For that reason, we suggest that data extracted like this should be tagged and that you should record whether the data was summarized across time, across spatially-independent samples (or different individuals), or across both. These factors may explain methodological heterogeneity in your dataset.

title: Continuous predictor
section: Discrete responses with a continuous predictor
text:
Discrete responses with a continuous predictor
Imagine you are conducting a meta-analysis concerned with factors driving nest success or failure in a seabird. Many of the studies use a discrete predictor, e.g., presence or absence of a predator. These types of data are naturally suited for lnOR or lnRR effect sizes. However, other studies report mortality in relationship to the abundance of that predator—e.g., the continuous manifestation of presence/absence.








Depending on your meta-analysis question you may very well want to extract this data and calculate a Zr correlation effect size, which can then be converted to lnOR (see here) and compared to your other lnOR discrete-predictor effect sizes. To do so, extract each point, which is an individual, and calculate Zr with the responses as a binary variable of 0 or 1.
This conversion is safe because presence/absence is a discretized version of abundance and because the unit of replication is the number of nests (or individuals) in both cases.

title: Continuous predictor
section: Proportion data with a continuous predictor
text:
Proportion data with a continuous predictor
You can imagine similar challenges where instead of 0 or 1 responses, the authors report % of a population:








You can calculate Zr directly between the predictor (temperature, x-axis) and the proportion alive (the y axis), directly.
However, each location on the x-axis actually represents a population of individuals, all of whom were monitored to determine the proportion alive. As such, simply calculating Zr directly from the proportion ignores population size and treats the number of surveys (or sites) as the unit of replication (n=10).
This can lead to a serious mismatch with the rest of your dataset—if the rest of your dataset is based the number of individuals as the unit of replication (like above)
To deal with this, the best option would be to convert the proportion data to binary response data based on the total number of individuals in each x-axis treatment—if this can be reconstructed from author reported summaries.
For example, if this figure reflects an experiment where each temperature treatment had 15 individuals, then you can multiply the survivorship at each temperature level by 15, and then expand this dataset to have a 0 or 1 for all 15 individuals per temperature treatment.
Let’s give it a try. dt is a data.table with a column for proportion alive and for temperature. We’ll calculate the number of living and dead individuals, make the dataset long so that these are in one column, and then duplicate the dataset to be one row per individual. text:
Mean±SD proportion data with continuous predictor
Now let’s look at a similar situation, except the figure is presenting mean±SD mortality across separate trials within each temperature treatment.








If we want our unit of replication to be based on the number of individuals, we need to try to reconstruct the underlying distributions behind each of these summarized trials. This will allow us to calculate a correlation across individuals for the binary response of being alive or dead, instead of across the mean per trial.
We also, of course need to figure out, from the text, the number of individuals and the number of trials (or sites, plots, etc) that the mean±sd were calculated from.






Note



A similar data structure could occur with discrete outcomes per plot instead of individuals with the number of sites/islands interchangeable with the number of trials.
An example would be the number of plots occupied by a species (the discrete outcome) per study site (the trial), which are sampled across some continuous gradient of interest.


To do this, we will do something similar as in the previous section. However we will use either the binomial or beta-binomial distribution instead of the normal distribution.

Click here for a full demonstration
To understand whether to use the binomial or beta-binomial distribution, we will check whether the observed (author-reported) standard deviation is greater than the theoretical standard deviation of the binomial distribution, which is defined by the proportion and the the number of individuals per trial.

theoretical_sd <- sqrt((dt$proportion_alive * (1 - dt$proportion_alive))/(dt$n_individuals))

nrow(dt[sd > theoretical_sd])

[1] 0


It looks like the reported standard deviations are all less than or equal to the theoretical standard deviation of the binomial family. So we can use the binomial distribution to generate the raw underyling data. See here for the equations and a fuller description, as well as how to generate data for beta-binomial distributed data (when \(sd_{reported} > sd_{theoretical}\)).
Now we’ll draw binomial data with the rbinom function. We specify size as number of individuals per trial (n_individuals in our dataset dt), n as number of trials (n_trials in our dataset), and p as the author reported mean proportion alive (proportion_alive). The function will return a numeric vector, with each element indicating the number of alive individuals per trial. With 3 trials, each vector should have a length of 3.






Warning



Note that reconstructing underlying data is an experimental method. Use carefully.


For a single temperature treatment, this looks like this:

rbinom(p = dt$proportion_alive[1],
       size = dt$n_individuals[1],
       n = dt$n_trials[1])

[1] 16 15 14


Each element of the vector reports the estimated number of individuals that survived of the 20 individuals in that trial.






Note



Note that if the number of individuals differed across trials within the same temperature treatment, you can provide a vector of values instead of a single value to the size argument:

rbinom(p = dt$proportion_alive[1],
       size = c(10, 15, 5),
       n = dt$n_trials[1])

[1] 5 9 3


However, in this case, we question whether the article’s authors should have summarized this data by mean±sd in the first place.


Now we’ll use a for loop to iterate over our dataset per temperature treatment. We’ll take the sum of the vector returned by rbbinom, which gives the total number of living individuals across the three trials.

y_expanded <- list()

for(i in 1:nrow(dt)){
  y_expanded[[i]] <- data.table(n_alive = sum(rbinom(p = dt$proportion_alive[i],
                                                     size = dt$n_individuals[i],
                                                     n = dt$n_trials[i])),
                                temperature = dt$temperature[i])
}

title: Simulating non-Gaussian data
text:
Reconstructing the underlying distributions that lurk beneath data summaries is one of the most interesting and potentially dangerous tricks in our meta-analysis toolkit. These cases are experimental and require further research yet also can do something very important: align the units of replication of the data underlying your meta-analysis.
These tools are for figures like this, which we have already described here:








Or, like this for an SMD effect size:








If the data in these figures (underlying each point) is normally distributed you can use rnorm to simulate the original dataset based on the means, standard deviations, and sample sizes (as our code in those sections demonstrated). This allows you to calculate effect sizes on results that may otherwise be unextractable. However, this assumes that data is normally distributed, which may be not be true in the case of ecological or evolutionary data.

To understand whether the underlying data can be drawn safely from the normal distribution, you need to think carefully about the data generating process.

Is the data discrete, e.g., count data or abundance data?


Abundance data generally follows a negative binomial or Poisson distribution. Data bounded between 0 and 1 (e.g., cover data) follows the Beta distribution.


What is the relationship between the means and reported error?


In normally distributed data the coefficient of variation (\(\frac{sd}{m}\)) should be <X. The variance (\(sd^2\)) of Poisson type data should be equal to the mean (which is unusual). In negative binomial data, the variance should be greater than the mean.*

Use these rules of thumb to help decide what distribution the underlying data is. Once you have a good idea, you then need to use distributionally specific formulas to convert the author-provided summary statistics (mean, standard deviation) to the distribution’s own parameters. For example, negative binomial uses size instead of standard deviation to describe its dispersion. Luckily, as we show below, converting standard deviation to size is possible.
Here is a table of the parameters necessary to simulate data in most distributions you’ll encounter during a meta-analysis, along with the formulas to convert standard deviation to these parameters.

Some studies report mean±sd (\(m±sd\)) proportions (or probabilities) across trials/sites/islands/years. For example, the mean proportion of nests that fledged across several islands or the mean proportion of seedlings that survived across plots.
You can readily meta-analyze this data using an SMD/lnRoM/Zmu type effect size with trials/sites/islands/years as the unit of replication, after transforming the mean and standard deviation (see here)
However, this type of data is naturally an lnOR type effect size, with a discrete outcome (e.g., fledged, survived) and if the rest of your dataset uses individual as the unit of replication, these effect sizes will be considerably underweighted and will be fundamentally incomparable.
However, it is possible to convert data summaries like this into the underlying binary outcomes using the binomial distribution. The binomial distribution describes the probability of success (\(p\)) across \(t\) trials (sites/islands/years) and \(n\) individuals. Note that \(m\) is usually used for number of trials in binomial formulas but, since we have been referring to means as \(m\), we will refer to number of trials as \(t\).
Doing so requires that you know the number of individuals (\(n\)), e.g. total number of nests or individuals monitored. There are ways to estimate the number of individuals but doing so assumes that \(p\) is equal across all trials, which is unlikely in the real world. We also suspect that most studies present the number of individuals (though potentially across all trials and not per trial/site/etc).
You can then draw binomial data in R, with size equivalent to the number of individuals and n equivalent to the number of trials/sites/islands. In the code below, we’re simulating data for an author-reported mean of 0.4, from 5 separate trials/sites/islands, each of which had 10 individuals:

n_individuals = 10
mean_proportion = 0.4
n_sites = 5
out <- rbinom(size = n_individuals, 
              p = mean_proportion, 
              n = n_sites)
out

[1] 2 5 2 3 3


Each element of the resulting vector is the number of individuals (of 10 total) that experienced the binomial outcome. We can now coerce this into a format that is compatible with calculating lnOR type effect sizes (with only one level of treatment).

dat <- data.table(n_fledged = sum(out),
                  n_failed = (n_individuals * n_sites) - sum(out))

You might note that the author-provided \(sd\) was ignored. This is because the binomial distribution assumes that variance is a direct result of the proportion (\(p\)) and number of individuals (\(n\)):
\[
\begin{aligned}
&Var(p) = \frac{p(1-p)}{n} \\
\end{aligned}
\]
For that reason, you should check whether the author-reported standard deviation is equal or less than the theoretical standard deviation of the binomial distribution. With \(\bar{p}\) as the reported mean proportion and \(n\) as the number of individuals, the theoretical \(sd_{theoretical}\) should be:
\[
\begin{aligned}
sd_{theoretical} = \sqrt{\frac{\bar{p}(1-\bar{p})}{n}}
\end{aligned}
\]
If the reported \(sd\) is larger than this, you should use the Beta-Binomial distribution instead. Or, consider analyzing this data, and similar data, separately as an SMD type effect size with the number of trials/sites as the unit of replication.
We demonstrated similar conversions for Zr type data here.

It is highly likely that the author-reported \(sd\) is larger than the theoretical binomial \(sd\). If this is the case, we can inject variance (\(sd^2\)) into the data generating process by using the Beta-Binomial distribution. To do so we need to calculate Beta distribution shape parameters (\(\alpha\) and \(\beta\)). This can be based on the following relationships, with \(m\) and \(sd\) as the author-reported mean and standard deviation:
\[\begin{aligned}
& Var = sd^2 \\
& r = (\frac{m(1-m)}{Var}) - 1\\
& \alpha = m * r \\
& \beta = (1-m) * r \\
\end{aligned}\] In R:

sd = 0.12
n_sites = 5

r <- (mean_proportion * (1 - mean_proportion) / var) - 1

alpha <- mean_proportion * r
beta  <- (1 - mean_proportion) * r

out <- rbbinom(n = n_sites, size = n_individuals, alpha = alpha, beta = beta)

title: Simulating non-Gaussian data
text:
To understand whether the underlying data can be drawn safely from the normal distribution, you need to think carefully about the data generating process.

Is the data discrete, e.g., count data or abundance data?


Abundance data generally follows a negative binomial or Poisson distribution. Data bounded between 0 and 1 (e.g., cover data) follows the Beta distribution.


What is the relationship between the means and reported error?


In normally distributed data the coefficient of variation (\(\frac{sd}{m}\)) should be <X. The variance (\(sd^2\)) of Poisson type data should be equal to the mean (which is unusual). In negative binomial data, the variance should be greater than the mean.*

Use these rules of thumb to help decide what distribution the underlying data is. Once you have a good idea, you then need to use distributionally specific formulas to convert the author-provided summary statistics (mean, standard deviation) to the distribution’s own parameters. For example, negative binomial uses size instead of standard deviation to describe its dispersion. Luckily, as we show below, converting standard deviation to size is possible.
Here is a table of the parameters necessary to simulate data in most distributions you’ll encounter during a meta-analysis, along with the formulas to convert standard deviation to these parameters.

ImportantSummarizing non-independent and independent data



In several sections through this tutorial we demonstrate or allude to reconstructing underlying data behind author summaries. This can align the unit of replication of the resulting effect sizes with the rest of your dataset.
However, one should be thoughtful and careful about the non-independence structures embedded within these summaries. The resulting effect size will be based on a mixture of more and less independent data. For example, in the time series above, there are two types of non-independence: the measurements through time and the summarized measurements within each time point.
Reconstructing the underlying data with rnorm, as we demonstrated above, and then summarizing by the mean±sd of each treatment group mixes these non-independence structures.
For that reason, we suggest that data extracted like this should be tagged and that you should record whether the data was summarized across time, across spatially-independent samples (or different individuals), or across both. These factors may explain methodological heterogeneity in your dataset. Note that similar mixtures of spatially, temporally, or spatiotemporally summarized data are also likely embedded within author-reported means±sds (which we also recommend recording)

This data format lends itself naturally to SMD/lnRoM/Zmu type effect sizes. If the unit of replication of the rest of your dataset is the number of individuals (or nests) then this effect size would have vastly less weight in your models (and should be analyzed separately).

title: An overview of effect sizes
text:
Alternative estimators
You’ll also notice, for example if looking at the documentation of escalc, that there are many many effect size estimators that are similar to the primary effect size flavors covered here yet have small differences that can be difficult to disentangle. These are often rarely used despite their potential utility to meta-analyses.
Some of these estimates can be lumped with the typical effect size flavors. Others cannot.
One of the most statistically important alternative flavors account for paired designs—i.e., non-independence between control and experimental groups. For example, before-after data or paired plot comparisons. These are common experimental designs in ecology and evolution but most meta-analyses do not take into account for this non-independence.
Some paired-design formulas produce effect sizes and sampling variance estimates that are comparable to those produced from unpaired formulas. In these cases, the effect size point estimate will be the same, or nearly the same, regardless of the paired/unpaired formulation. However, the sampling variance for the paired design will be lower—which will give paired design data more weight in downstream meta-analytic models.
We try to clear up this confusion in the appendix with some charts of compatibility between the different estimators in escalc.

title: Differences in magnitude between two groups
text:
The effect sizes that we’ve described in depth in this tutorial have concerned the direction and magnitude of mean relationships between two variables.
However, there are also effect sizes to describe the absolute magnitude of differences between groups (lnM), to describe differences in variability (or heteroscedasticity) between two groups (lnVR and lnCVR) and effect sizes to summarize single-group means and proportions. Extracting data for these effect sizes should be fundamentally similar as the other effect size types that this tutorial was dedicated to. We here briefly discuss these effect sizes, their assumptions, and how to calculate them in R.

title: Differences in magnitude between two groups

Differences in magnitude
lnM is an effect size that describes the absolute difference between two groups, which is often relevant in evolutionary research where the direction of difference between two populations or species is not of interest relative to absolute magnitude of differences (Nakagawa et al. 2026a). This effect size replaces earlier efforts which took the absolute value of SMD (or ‘folded-normal SMD’).
To calculate lnM, you need the sample sizes (\(n_1\), \(n_2\)), means (\(m_1\), \(m_2\)), and standard deviations (\(sd_1\), \(sd_2\)) for two discrete groups, similar as when calculating SMD or lnRoM effect sizes. Note that there is also a paired version of lnM that requires only 1 sample size (\(n\)) and \(rho\)—the estimated correlation between the two groups. As with other paired effect sizes, since \(rho\) is usually unreported, you can use values of 0.5 or 0.8 (and conduct sensitivity analyses!).
