title: Continuous predictors: assumptions and interpretation
text:
As you have seen so far in this guide, effect sizes are not trivial things. Together, point estimates and sampling variances are small statistical models with their own numerical assumptions, properties, and quirks. Understanding these assumptions is essential if you want to conduct a proper and robust meta-analysis, and if you want to correctly interpret these effect sizes and the outputs of meta-analytic models.
In this section, we discuss effect sizes for describing the relationship strength between two continuous variables. These are known as measures of association. While the Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient (\(r\)) is the most intuitive and widely reported metric in primary studies, its mathematical properties make it problematic for direct meta-analytic pooling. Instead, we will dive into the elegant statistical world of Fisher’s Z-transformed correlation coefficient (\(Z_r\)), our variance-stabilizing alternative.

Why can’t we just pool raw correlations?
Should make clear that many studies don’t even report \(r\), they just plot scatterplots (that they might have analyzed with linear models)
When primary studies report their results, they often present Pearson’s correlation coefficient (\(r\)). It is an appealing effect size: it carries no units, so a correlation between body mass and clutch size can be compared directly against one between soil nitrogen and plant diversity (if that makes sense to be compared, which is another question). It runs from \(-1\) (a perfect negative linear association) through \(0\) (no linear association) to \(+1\) (a perfect positive linear association).
I think we should also add how \(r\) captures both relationship and variance in a single value, which can be confusing if your last stats class was ages ago…
Convenient as it is, the raw correlation coefficient has three mathematical properties that sit awkwardly with the assumptions of standard meta-analytic models. All three trace back to a single issue: \(r\) is bounded by \(-1\) and \(+1\), and statistical estimates behave badly near hard limits.

The estimate gets squeezed against the ceiling. When the true correlation in the population is near zero, repeated studies scatter symmetrically around it. When the true correlation is strong, say \(+0.8\), there is simply less room to overshoot than to undershoot, because no estimate can exceed \(+1\). The spread of plausible estimates becomes lopsided, with a long tail on the low side. The practical cost is that confidence intervals calculated the usual way assume a symmetric spread, so they end up miscalibrated and can even extend beyond \(1\), which does not make sense. Separately, and through a different route, \(r\) is a slightly shrunken estimate of the true correlation. It is pulled toward zero, whatever its sign. That shrinkage is small (for a true correlation of \(0.5\) measured on \(20\) individuals, roughly \(0.01\)), but it is the reason unbiased alternatives to \(r\) exist (Olkin and Pratt 1958).
Precision is tangled up with the result. Meta-analysis weights each study by its precision, and this only works if precision is governed by something independent of the answer, such as sample size. For correlations it is not. The sampling variance of \(r\) is

\[
v_i = \frac{(1 - r_i^2)^2}{n_i - 1}
\tag{1}\]
which contains the correlation itself. The larger the correlation a study happens to report, the smaller its variance and the heavier its weight. A study that overestimated the correlation by chance is therefore rewarded with extra influence, and the pooled estimate is dragged away from zero. Notice that this pushes in the opposite direction to the shrinkage in point 1, above. The same entanglement distorts funnel plots and inflates the false-positive rate of Egger’s test for funnel asymmetry. The scatter narrows toward large correlations for reasons that have nothing to do with genuine precision.


Small samples make matters worse. Meta-analytic models assume each study’s estimate is drawn from a bell-shaped distribution around the true value. For correlations, that approximation holds up well with large samples and modest effects, and it breaks down when the sample is small and the correlation is strong—the combination most familiar to anyone working with a dozen populations or a handful of species.

To solve these issues, Fisher proposed a variance-stabilizing, normalizing transformation (Fisher 1921, Borenstein et al. 2021).
The statistical mechanics of \(Z_r\)

1. Fisher’s \(Z\) transformation (the point estimate)
Fisher’s transformation stretches the bounded \([-1, +1]\) interval across the entire number line, pushing the ceilings out to infinity so that estimates are no longer squeezed against them. Formally, it is the inverse hyperbolic tangent (\(\text{atanh}\)):
\[
y_i = Z_{r_i} = \text{atanh}(r_i) = \frac{1}{2} \ln\left(\frac{1 + r_i}{1 - r_i}\right)
\tag{2}\]
Should the second = sign by a \(\approx\)?
Correlations near zero barely move. Correlations near the boundaries are stretched dramatically. The result is a distribution that is close to symmetric and close to normal for samples of roughly \(10\) or more.
2. The sampling variance
The real beauty of Fisher’s transformation lies in its sampling variance. After transformation, the sampling variance depends on sample size and nothing else:
\[v_i = \text{Var}(Z_{r_i}) = \frac{1}{n_i - 3} \tag{3}\]
The effect size has vanished from the variance entirely. Studies are now weighted purely by how much data they collected, which is exactly the assumption meta-analytic models were built on. Symmetry and approximate normality come along for free.






NoteThe variance formula assumes bivariate normality



Fisher’s variance is derived assuming the two variables follow a bivariate normal distribution. This means both variables are normal but covary. See here to explore this distribution.
When the underlying data are strongly non-normal (heavy tailed) abundance counts, or ratios with a few extreme values, the true sampling variance can be noticeably larger than \(1/(n_i - 3)\), and standard errors will be too optimistic (Kowalski 1972, Hawkins 1989). This is a further reason to prefer robust variance estimation (see below) when your evidence base is built on skewed ecological data.
I guess this means that you can’t do funky things, like calculate Zr for continuous responses and a discrete predictor?


3. Back-transformation to \(r\)

We conduct all statistical modeling, random-effects estimation, and moderator tests in the \(Z_r\) metric, but \(Z_r\) values are difficult to interpret conceptually. An effect size of \(Z_r = 1.1\) means very little to our brain until we convert it back to \(r = 0.8\). We therefore back-transform final pooled estimates from our meta-analytic models, and the confidence intervals, to the intuitive correlation scale using the hyperbolic tangent (\(\tanh\)):
\[r = \tanh(Z_r) = \frac{e^{2 Z_r} - 1}{e^{2 Z_r} + 1} \tag{4}\]






WarningBack-transformation is not a neutral operation



Because the conversion from \(Z_r\) to \(r\) is curved rather than straight, back-transforming a pooled estimate does not return the average of the underlying correlations. It returns something closer to their median, and the gap between the two widens as between-study heterogeneity grows. In ecology and evolution, where heterogeneity is usually substantial, a back-transformed mean will typically exaggerate the magnitude of the true average correlation.
Three practical consequences:

Interval bounds back-transform safely. Because the transformation preserves rank order, converting the two ends of a confidence or prediction interval gives valid bounds on the \(r\) scale. So, convert the endpoints, never the standard error.
Heterogeneity does not back-transform at all. Report \(\tau^2\), \(I^2\), and prediction intervals on the \(Z_r\) scale, or convert the prediction interval endpoints only. There is no meaningful “\(\tau^2\) in correlation units.”
Word your conclusion carefully. “The pooled effect corresponds to a correlation of 0.42” is defensible; “the average correlation across studies was 0.42” is not, once heterogeneity is appreciable.

Some authors (notably the Hunter–Schmidt tradition; Hunter and Schmidt (2014); Field (2001)) respond to this by pooling raw correlations with sample-size weights instead. We use Fisher’s \(Z_r\) throughout this guide because it solves three problems at once, but the choice is genuinely contested and worth considering.


Code and formula pairing: implementation in R
Let’s look at how to implement these calculations in R using metafor::escalc and basic math.
Note that in many cases, the \(Z_r\) effect sizes that you calculate in a meta-analysis will involve multiple steps. Few studies report \(r\) directly. Instead many of those studies will present scatterplot visualizations, which they analyze with linear models. To calculate \(r\) (the precursor to \(Z_r\)), you’ll have to extract the points from the scatterplot (or find their raw data) and calculate \(r\) across the points.
As such, your raw dataset will be long, with a row per measurement point and an ID to specify the summarization group to calculate \(r\). The sample size (\(n\)) will be the number of rows.
Once \(r\) and \(n\) are calculated the operation is simple. We’ll here show both calculating manually and with escalc.

# Simple demonstration of Zr transformation and back-transformation in R

# Let's say we have extracted a correlation of r = 0.6 from a study of n = 50
r_val <- 0.6
n_val <- 50

# 1. Manual Fisher's Z transformation
z_manual <- 0.5 * log((1 + r_val) / (1 - r_val))
var_manual <- 1 / (n_val - 3)

# 2. Using escalc from metafor
dat_example <- data.frame(ri = r_val, ni = n_val)
dat_zr <- escalc(measure = "ZCOR", ri = ri, ni = ni, data = dat_example)

print(paste("Manual Z:", round(z_manual, 4)))

[1] "Manual Z: 0.6931"

print(paste("escalc Z (yi):", round(dat_zr$yi[1], 4)))

[1] "escalc Z (yi): 0.6931"

print(paste("escalc Z (vi):", round(dat_zr$vi[1], 4)))

[1] "escalc Z (vi): 0.0213"

# 3. Back-transformation using tanh
r_back <- tanh(z_manual)
print(paste("Back-transformed r:", round(r_back, 4)))

[1] "Back-transformed r: 0.6"








NoteFisher’s \(Z\) in metafor



The metafor package (Viechtbauer 2010) implements Fisher’s \(Z\) transformation via the measure code "ZCOR". This is the measure you want for the workflow in this chapter.
You may also encounter "UCOR", which applies the Olkin-Pratt correction (Olkin and Pratt 1958) for the small-sample shrinkage described above. Be aware that "UCOR" returns a corrected raw correlation, not a transformed one. So it fixes the shrinkage while leaving the variance-effect entanglement fully intact. It is not an upgraded version of "ZCOR", and the two should not be mixed within a single analysis. In general, we know of few cases where "UCOR" should be used instead of "ZCOR".



Click here to see a visual demonstration of the transformation stretching effect
Let’s plot how \(r\) maps to \(Z_r\). Notice how the relationship is nearly a straight line around zero but curves sharply as it approaches the boundaries of \(-1\) and \(+1\):

r_seq <- seq(-0.99, 0.99, by = 0.01)
zr_seq <- atanh(r_seq)

plot_data <- data.frame(r = r_seq, zr = zr_seq)

ggplot(plot_data
  , aes(x = r
      ,y = zr)
  ) +
  geom_line(color = "blue", linewidth = 1) +
  theme_minimal() + 
  labs(title = "Fisher's r-to-Z transformation"
    , x = "Raw correlation (r)"
    , y = "Fisher's Z (Zr)") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray")







Not all correlations are comparable
DAMN, this is useful and fuck, didn’t think of that…Thanks Ed!!
Before converting anything, check that the correlations you have extracted are estimating the same quantity. Three common mismatches will quietly corrupt an otherwise careful meta-analysis.
Partial correlations are not zero-order correlations. A study reporting the association between temperature and growth rate after controlling for body size is reporting a different parameter from a study reporting the raw association. Pooling the two together answers no clear question. If you must include partial correlations, flag them, model them as a moderator, and adjust the sample size to account for the covariates that were controlled for (the variance is closer to \(1/(n_i - k_i - 3)\), where \(k_i\) is the number of control variables; Fisher (1924); Aloe and Thompson (2013)).
Range restriction shrinks correlations (Thorndike 1949, Sackett and Yang 2000). A study sampling across a narrow elevational band will report a weaker correlation than one spanning the full gradient, even if the underlying biology is identical. Where you can, record range or standard deviation of the predictor and use it as a moderator.
Measurement error shrinks correlations too (Spearman 1904, Hunter and Schmidt 2014). Noise proxies attenuate associations toward zero. If reliability estimates are available for some studies and not others, this becomes a source of heterogeneity you cannot see.
Handling ranked correlations: Spearman’s \(\rho\) and Kendall’s \(\tau\)

When voyaging through the literature, you will inevitably encounter studies that present raw data, scatterplots, or matrices, that need to be analyzed as \(Z_r\) but are based on ranks rather than raw values. Or you will encounter studies that do not report Pearson’s \(r\). Instead, because their data were non-normal or ranked, they reported Spearman’s rank correlation (\(\rho\) or \(r_s\)) or Kendall’s tau (\(\tau\)).
Maybe we should define these?
Because these metrics are based on ranks rather than raw values, their numeric scales are slightly compressed compared to Pearson’s \(r\). To include these studies in your meta-analysis, you can apply the following transformations to approximate their Pearson equivalents:
Spearman’s \(\rho\) to Pearson’s \(r\):
\[r \approx 2 \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6} \rho\right) \tag{5}\]
Kendall’s \(\tau\) to Pearson’s \(r\):
\[r \approx \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} \tau\right) \tag{6}\]
Both formulas assume the underlying data are bivariate normal (Kendall 1948, Rupinski and Dunlap 1996), which is very often the assumption the original authors doubted when they chose a rank method in the first place. Treat the conversions as approximations.
A useful refinement: once converted and Fisher-transformed, an effect size originating from Spearman’s \(\rho\) is slightly noisier than one originating from Pearson’s \(r\). Because ranks discard some metric information, converted rank correlations have slightly lower statistical efficiency than Pearson correlations, inflating the sampling variance of \(Z_r\) by about 6% under bivariate normality (Fieller et al. 1957, Myers and Sirois 2004):
\[v_i \approx \frac{1.06}{n_i - 3} \tag{7}\]
As such, these converted effect sizes will have less influence on your meta-analytic models, which, at least is a conservative type of error.






ImportantSensitivity analyses as best practice



Never treat these conversions as magic solutions. Approximations introduce uncertainty. Always flag converted effect sizes in your dataset (e.g., is_converted = TRUE) and run sensitivity analyses. Specifically, run your meta-analytic models both with and without the converted Spearman and Kendall correlations. If your overall effect size or its uncertainty shifts substantially, you must report this and be cautious in your interpretations.


The “unit of replication” obsession
A central theme of our guide is the unit of replication. When calculating and meta-analyzing measures of association, ensuring that the unit of replication aligns across studies is paramount. Mismatches in the level of replication will alter your sample size, your sampling variance, and consequently how much influence each study has on your pooled result.
Consider a study examining the correlation between soil nitrogen and plant diversity:


Study A measures the correlation across 50 individual quadrats (\(n = 50\)).

Study B measures the correlation across 5 distinct geographic sites, where each site represents the pooled average of 10 quadrats (\(n = 5\)).

Even if both studies report an identical correlation of \(r = 0.5\), Study A carries roughly 47 units of weight against Study B’s 2. A difference of more than twentyfold (!), driven entirely by a decision about what counts as a replicate. If site is the true independent unit of replication, treating Study A’s quadrats as independent replicates is pseudoreplication (Hurlbert 1984).






NoteWeights are not simply \(n - 3\)



The figures above assume a common-effects model, where a study’s weight is one over its sampling variance. In the random-effects and multilevel models you will actually fit, weight is one over the sampling variance plus the between-study variance \(\tau^2\). That extra term acts as a floor on everyone’s uncertainty and compresses the differences between studies considerably: with a moderate \(\tau^2\) of \(0.1\), the twentyfold gap above shrinks to roughly fivefold. Large studies still dominate, but far less absolutely than the raw sample sizes suggest.


Before running your models:

Identify the true, independent unit of replication for each study.
Standardize or aggregate correlations where necessary to avoid inflating sample sizes.
When in doubt, perform sensitivity analysis by adjusting sample sizes to reflect conservative biological units of replication.

Non-independence, matrices, and tagging
Correlation coefficients frequently violate the assumption of independence. Two main traps exist in continuous predictor meta-analyses:
1. Pairwise correlation matrices (the melting trap)
Primary studies often present a correlation matrix comparing multiple traits or environmental factors. Meta-analysts sometimes “melt” these matrices and include all pairwise correlations as separate effect sizes.
For example, imagine that a study reports a pairwise matrix of grooming interactions between individuals, which is thought to be a predictor of defense interactions between individuals. Melting these matrices allows you to calculate \(r\). However, the observations in that matrix are non-independent as each individual is repeated multiple times (for each interaction with other individuals).






WarningMelted matrices cause non-independence that grows quadratically



If a study measures 5 traits on a single set of individuals, it generates \(\frac{5 \times (5-1)}{2} = 10\) pairwise correlations. Those 10 correlations share the exact same subjects. Treating them as independent data points inflates your Type I error rate, because the model behaves as though you had ten times more information than you actually collected.


To handle this non-independence:

Use multilevel meta-analysis with a random effect for study or paper identity to absorb shared variance (Noble et al. 2017).
Where the same individuals contribute to several correlations, construct an explicit variance-covariance matrix with metafor::rcalc rather than relying on random effects alone.
Combine either approach with robust variance estimation (Hedges et al. 2010, Pustejovsky and Tipton 2018) (metafor::robust, or the clubSandwich package) so that your standard errors remain trustworthy even if the assumed covariance structure is imperfect.

What do you do if some studies require rcalc but others do not? As it provides a pan-dataset variance-covariance matrix
Should link to tutorials on these methods
2. Spatial and temporal flagging
Continuous predictors in ecology and evolution often vary across spatial and temporal grains. Always record and flag metadata for:


Spatial grain: e.g., local plot size, regional \(\text{km}^2\).

Temporal grain: e.g., seasonal correlation, decadal trend.

Flag groupings: flag studies sharing common study sites, common control subjects, or common experimental treatments.

Interpretation and benchmarks: what does \(r\) mean?
When interpreting your pooled effect size, you may encounter the traditional benchmarks proposed by Jacob Cohen (1988):








Effect size class
Correlation coefficient (\(r\))
Variance explained (\(r^2\))
Interpretation



Small
\(0.1\)
\(1\%\)
Subtle effect, barely visible to the naked eye.


Medium
\(0.3\)
\(9\%\)
Visible to a careful observer; typical of many social and ecological processes.


Large
\(0.5\)
\(25\%\)
Prominent relationship; easily detectable.



These labels were offered by Cohen as a fallback for researchers with no domain knowledge to draw on, and he said so explicitly. The interpretation of effect sizes is highly context-dependent:

In evolutionary ecology, natural selection operates on tiny margins. A correlation of \(r = 0.05\)—explaining a quarter of one percent of the variance—can be strongly adaptive and shape survival over generations (Kingsolver et al. 2001, Nakagawa and Santos 2012).
In biomedical research, regular aspirin consumption has an effect on heart attack risk equivalent to \(r = 0.034\). This explains about one tenth of one percent of the variance, yet translates to thousands of lives saved annually (Rosenthal 1990).

Never apply Cohen’s benchmarks blindly. Always interpret your pooled correlations in the context of the biology, the decision costs, and the practical implications of the phenomenon.
Recommended workflow for continuous predictors
Fantastic!!!
To ensure your meta-analysis is rigorous, stick to the following workflow:


Extract raw data: Record the correlation, its sample size, the type of correlation reported, whether it is zero-order or partial, and the unit of replication.

Screen for comparability: Set aside or flag partial correlations, and note any study with obvious range restriction or unreliable measurement.

Standardize conversions: Convert any Spearman’s \(\rho\) or Kendall’s \(\tau\) to Pearson’s \(r\) equivalents. Flag these.

Calculate Fisher’s \(Z_r\): Transform raw and converted correlations using metafor::escalc(measure = "ZCOR").

Address non-independence: Check for melted matrices and shared subjects. Nest non-independent effect sizes within study using multilevel random effects.

Run models: Fit multilevel random-effects models in the \(Z_r\) metric, paired with robust variance estimation.

Test sensitivity: Re-run models excluding converted metrics, small-sample outliers, or pseudoreplicated studies.

Back-transform for reporting: Convert pooled estimates and interval endpoints back to \(r\) using tanh. Keep heterogeneity statistics on the \(Z_r\) scale, and word your conclusions to reflect what the back-transformed value actually represents.

title: Discrete groups with continuous outcomes
text:
These are among the most commonly used effect size types in meta-analyses. These effect sizes compare a continuous response variable between two discrete categorical predictors (e.g., Control vs Experiment). By continuous, we mean a measurement summarized by its central tendency (mean, median) and dispersion (variance, standard deviation, standard error) across replicates. These replicates are the sample size.
The primary effect sizes that can be calculated with this data are standardized mean difference (SMD) and log-transformed ratio of means (lnRoM). Please see here for a more thorough description of these effect sizes, their assumptions, and their interpretation. In general, the extraction for these effect sizes is similar. However, as you will see, some data types constrain you to only using SMD because of values ≤ 0, which only SMD can handle.

title: Discrete groups with continuous outcomes
text:
SMD dream material
We’ll start with the simplest figure types, mostly in order to contrast with more complex types. If you’re using metaDigitise() to extract data (Pick et al. 2018), the function will guide you through calibrating the axes and selecting the top of the error bars and the top of the bars themselves (the mean). If the figure reports standard error (\(se\)), metaDigitise() will convert it automatically to standard deviation (\(sd\)). Always be aware of what the error type is.








Box plots are also straightforward and involve extracting the minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile, and maximum values. metaDigitise() will walk you through that extraction and will automatically convert the interquartile range and median to mean±SD.








It’s also common to see figures like this with more complex non-independence structures. These can be dealt with by digitizing only the final time point or by controlling for non-independence with random effects (see here for a brief discussion of these issues).








Let’s move on to more complex situations.






Important3-dimensional plots



There was a brief period in the 1990s when these became popular. 3D plots were often of histograms. but many other types existed, including bar charts, etc.
We won’t discuss these much here, we just want to acknowledge your pain if you come across one. Hopefully the general plot designs will be similar to those covered in this tutorial. We believe that WebPlotDigitizer has options to calibrate 3D plots. Alternatively, LLMs are likely able to extract this data.

title: Discrete groups with continuous outcomes
text:
Histograms
It’s also common to see the outcome variable of the two discrete predictor groups plotted as separate histograms:








metaDigitise() luckily has built-in functionality for dealing with histograms. The function will guide you through each step, which requires calibrating the axes and then clicking on the left and right corners of each bar. It’ll then convert the extracted distributions into means±sd.

Proportion data (0-1) bounded without error
Sometimes SMD/lnRoM design types will present the total % of a population for a study design that is otherwise indistinguishable from other SMD/lnRoM studies in your dataset. For example, instead of recording mean mortality ± SD across survey plots, a study may present total mortality across all plots or individuals.
This data is derived from the binomial distribution, where standard deviation is directly related to the mean. As such, mean±SD can be extracted from a proportions with the following formulas, where \(p\) is the proportion, \(m\) is the mean, \(sd\) is standard deviation, and \(N_{total}\) is the population size??.

\[\begin{aligned}
&sd = p * (1-p) \\
&m = p*N_{total}?? \\
\end{aligned}\]
An alternative to is to use these values to calculate discrete response data for an lnOR type effect size. This may be a better option, especially if this maintains a comparable unit of replication with the rest of your dataset. We simulate a similar example, albeit for a Zr effect size, here

title: Discrete groups with continuous outcomes
text:
Mean±sd proportion data (0-1)
Means±SD bounded between 0 and 1, however, are also challenged by numeric properties: variance tends to retreat to zero when the mean approaches 0 or 1 (Macartney et al. 2022).
To resolve this, you need to transform both the means and the standard deviations, using an arcsin-square root transformation on the mean and an equation derived using the delta method on the standard deviation (see Macartney et al. (2022)). Where \(m\) is the group mean and \(sd\) is its standard deviation:
\[\begin{aligned}
&m' = arcsin(\sqrt{m})\\
&sd' = \sqrt{\frac{sd^2}{4m(1-m)}}\\
\end{aligned}\]
In R:

m = 0.7
sd = 0.1

m_trans <- asin(m)
sd_trans <- sqrt(sd^2 / (4*m * (1-m)))

c("transformed_mean" = m_trans, "transformed_sd" = sd_trans)

transformed_mean   transformed_sd 
       0.7753975        0.1091089 


And then calculate your effect sizes as normal with the transformed values (\(m'\) and \(sd'\)). Note that your sample size will be the number of sites this proportion was calculated across.






CautionReconstructing binomial data from means±sd



Proportion data is, at its root, discrete-outcome data, like that naturally handled by lnOR effect sizes. It is possible to reconstruct the underlying discrete-outcome data from author-reported means±sd across trials/sites/islands/etc, which allows you to calculate an lnOR type effect size.
This can help align the unit of replication of this effect size with the rest of your dataset, if the rest of your data treats number of individuals as the unit of replication. Analyzing mean±sd of proportion data with an SMD/lnRoM effect size would likely treat the number of trials/sites/islands/plots as the unit of replication instead, which is likely to underweight this effect size in your models.
To reconstruct the raw binary outcomes from author reported means and sd, see our explanation here and a more general tutorial about reconstructing various data types here

Differences
Some studies used paired designs where, instead of reporting each pair separately, they subtract the paired samples from each other and report mean±error of the difference.








To deal with this data, we’ll extract the boxplot with metaDigitise(), which will convert the median±interquartile range to mean±SD. We will then consider the control group to have a mean of 0. However, you have only one measurement of error. For this reason, you’ll have to pretend that the control error is the same as the treatment error.

Note that since lnRoM cannot accept negative values or 0s, you have no choice but to use SMD for this type of data. If the difference was positive, you could use lnRoM, after adding a small constant to the mean of the control group.
Also, given that this is paired data, you should use a paired formulation of SMD or lnRoM. Note that you have to specify \(r\) (ri in escalc) for this. We recommend using the values of 0.5 or 0.8 and conducting sensitivity tests with both options.

eff_size(x1 = -8.11, sd1 = 1.27, 
        x2 = 0, sd2 = 1.27, 
        n = 15, r = 0.8,
        paired = TRUE,
        verbose = FALSE,
        effect_type = "SMD")

# r = 0.5
eff_size(x1 = -8.11, sd1 = 1.27, 
        x2 = 0, sd2 = 1.27, 
        n = 15, r = 0.5,
        paired = TRUE,
        verbose = FALSE,
        effect_type = "SMD")

title: Discrete groups with continuous outcomes
section: Results reported as an effect size itself
text:
Results reported as an effect size itself
One common situation is for studies to report their results as an effect size itself (e.g., SMD or lnRoM). These could be extracted directly as your effect size except that in our experience these studies rarely report a measure of dispersion (sampling variance, or SD or SE which could be converted to variance).
If a measure of error is reported then you can use these effect sizes directly or convert them to your target effect size. See here on how to convert between effect size types.
If a measurement of error is provided, then you can extract the data as is, and convert that error to sampling variance. For example, if SMD ± standard error was plotted, the sampling variance is \[vi = SE^2\].
If a study reports standardized mean differences (e.g., Cohen’s d), which is uncorrected estimator of SMD, you can use escalc to convert it to Hedges' g, the dominant estimator of SMD by specifying Cohen’s d as the di argument:

escalc(measure = "SMD",
       di = 5, 
       n1i = 10, n2i = 10)


      yi     vi 
1 4.7882 0.7732 


In many other cases, there’s nothing you can do but email the authors and hope they have their raw data.

title: Discrete groups with continuous outcomes
text:
Before-after-control-impact designs
Before-after control-impact (BACI) designs are gold standard experimental designs. Yet most meta-analyses ignore the before treatment and only extract and analyze the ‘after’ treatments. Here is a BACI figure:








In this case, only extracting and analyzing the ‘after’ data isn’t a big deal, because the differences in the ‘before’ groups in the control and treatment are minimal.
However, what about a more problematic result, where there’s a big difference in before conditions between the control and treatment?








What do you do about something like that? Do you just exclude the study?
The best way to deal with this data is to calculate the difference between the means of the before and after groups for each treatment of interest.
Then use the standard deviation from the after treatment group. You could alternatively use the standard deviation from the before group, but we’re not sure how to justify this (you might know though).
Since the treatment groups themselves are not paired, you’d use an unpaired estimator formula.
Since your values may be negative, you’ll most likely have to use SMD. Imagine the object dt below is your raw extracted data:

dt

           m        sd before_after control_impact
       <num>     <num>       <fctr>         <char>
1:  7.444814 0.8790703        after        control
2: 13.871720 0.7661697        after         impact
3:  3.000000 1.2263422       before        control
4:  7.975997 1.0513753       before         impact


First, we reshape the data so that you can subtract the before/after treatments:

dt.wide <- dcast(data = dt,
                 control_impact ~ before_after,
                 value.var = c("m", "sd"))

Then subtract the means and select just the “after” standard deviation (st_after):

dt.wide[, difference := m_after - m_before]

dt.wide <- dt.wide[, sd := sd_after]

Now, drop the columns you don’t need, cast wide again by your treatment column (control_impact) and calculate your effect size.

dt.final <- dcast(dt.wide[, .(control_impact, difference, sd)],
                  . ~ control_impact,
                  value.var = c("difference", "sd"))

escalc(measure = "SMD",
       m1i = difference_impact, m2i = difference_control,
       n1i = 15, n2i = 15,
       sd1i = sd_impact, sd2i = sd_control,
       data = dt.final)


  . difference_control difference_impact sd_control sd_impact     yi     vi 
1 .           4.444814          5.895723  0.8790703 0.7661697 1.7120 0.1822 


Note that these 4 group designs may appear in other contexts than pre and post and can be fairly in common in ecological field experiments. For example, to understand if reintroduced wild dogs affect vegetation by reducing dik-dik browsing and abundance, Ford et al. (2015) placed controls and exclosures in areas with and without wild dogs, predicting that the difference between controls and exclosures would be greatest where there are no wild dogs.








In this case, you’d do the same as above. As you can see, when dealing with this type of data, lnRoM often becomes unusable because of negative values. Instead you have to use SMD.

text:
% Change
Sometimes BACI type data is presented directly as percent change, which saves us some of the steps above.

title: Discrete groups with continuous outcomes
text:
Discrete x discrete crossed design
Sometimes you are interested explicitly in interactions between two treatments. In most studies one of the treatments you are interested in would otherwise be a moderator (e.g., not crossed with the main experimental comparison), however in others you find a fully crossed design. What do you do about that?








In these cases, you’ll need to simply record these crossed moderators in separate columns in your dataset.

title: Discrete groups with continuous outcomes
text:
Continuous x discrete crossed design
However, sometimes interactions will be between continuous and discrete variables:








In this case, you could extract each point for the control group and the treatment group and calculate mean±SD across the continuous variable. But, if the continuous variable was a key moderator of interest in your analysis, it’d be lost from your meta-analysis.
Alternatively, you could calculate two Zr effect sizes, one for the ‘control group’ and one for the ‘treatment group’. The control group and moderator factor would then be a moderator—if this is how the rest of your dataset is designed.
As you can see, there might be no perfect solution. Care and thought are necessary to make this type of data comparable to other effect sizes in your dataset.

title: Discrete groups with continuous outcomes
section: Time series with a binary predictor
text:
Time series with a binary predictor
Sometimes the data is presented as a time series with a discrete intervention at one point in the time series, such as the introduction or eradication of a species. For example:








In the case above, you should extract the response of interest for each group (Present versus Eradicated), calculate mean±SD for each group, and then calculate SMD or lnRoM with the paired estimator. The sample size would be the number of individual points per group.
However, you’ll often see cases like this as well, with \(<3\) measurements for one of the factor groups (making SMD impossible to calculate):








In this case, your best bet will be to calculate a Zr effect size with a binary continuous predictor of 0 or 1 (see sec). The resulting effect size could be converted to SMD.
Note that summarizing time series data may often create summary statistics that are less independent than data that may derive from separate replicates. Record these summaries for use in sensitivity analysis. See our discussion here and Noble et al. (2017).

title: Discrete groups with continuous outcomes
text:
Time series with error bars
However, what do you do if each of these measurements has associated error?








There is no way to pair any of these samples except for the final measurement for the first treatment (“Present”) and the first measurement of the second treatment (“Eradicated”). This is defensible.
Alternatively, you can draw the underlying data based on sample size, group mean, and standard deviation extracted from the figure. This presents its own problems but is maybe better than giving up (which you should probably do. Go take a nap, sweet boy).
This should use the underlying data generating process of the response. If the response is normally distributed, or close enough, then you can use the R base function rnorm. If the data is not normally distributed then you can do a similar process, generating data from the underlying data generating process (see here).
This will produce a longer dataset, with a row for every estimated sample. You’d then calculate the group mean, standard deviation, and total sample size for the binary predictor of interest, in this case “Eradicated” versus “Present”. You can also do a similar process to calculate Zr, if a correlation includes error bars (see several examples here).






Warning



Note that reconstructing underlying data is an experimental method. Use carefully.

Voila, a dataset that constructs group means that are comparable, with an accurate sample size and pooled standard deviation. If the underlying data generating process is not normal (which is likely the case for ecological data, especially abundance data), then you probably want to use a negative binomial distribution to generate data.
The treatment variable (status) in this simulated dataset is paired, which should be reflected in your effect size estimator choice. See here for descriptions of paired estimators for SMD and lnRoM
Unfortunately, if the sample size for each of the points in the figure above is unknown, then your best option if the number of groups is ≥3, is to ignore the standard deviation and calculate a new mean from each point for the two SMD comparison groups. Or, if the number of groups is <3, to calculate Zr from just the group means per point (ignoring the standard deviation).
Remember that these choices severely affect your unit of replication and should be accounted for in your modeling approach.






ImportantSummarizing non-independent and independent data



In several sections through this tutorial we demonstrate or allude to reconstructing underlying data behind author summaries. This can align the unit of replication of the resulting effect sizes with the rest of your dataset.
However, one should be thoughtful and careful about the non-independence structures embedded within these summaries. The resulting effect size will be based on a mixture of more and less independent data. For example, in the time series above, there are two types of non-independence: the measurements through time and the summarized measurements within each time point.
Reconstructing the underlying data with rnorm, as we demonstrated above, and then summarizing by the mean±sd of each treatment group mixes these non-independence structures.
For that reason, we suggest that data extracted like this should be tagged and that you should record whether the data was summarized across time, across spatially-independent samples (or different individuals), or across both. These factors may explain methodological heterogeneity in your dataset. Note that similar mixtures of spatially, temporally, or spatiotemporally summarized data are also likely embedded within author-reported means±sds (which we also recommend recording).
A potentially better approach would be to generate the data with MASS:mvrnorm and specify individual correlations within each group (rho), which could be set to 0.8.

text:
From the t statistic
Calculating SMD from test statistics depends on whether the data come from a paired design (in which case df = n-1) or an independent two-sample design (df = n_1 + n_2 - 2). This is the formula for calculating SMD from a unpaired, two-sample design t test statistic:
\[\begin{aligned}
&d=t*\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}} \\
&J= 1 - \frac{3}{4(n_1 + n_2 - 2) - 1} \\
&g=J*d \\
&Var(g) = \frac{n_1 + n_2}{n_1 n_2} + \frac{g^2}{2(n_1 + n_2 - 2)} \\
\end{aligned}\]
In escalc you simply specify the t statistic (with ti), as well as sample sizes for each group (n1, n2) and use measure “SMD”, which will return the unpaired SMD estimate.

n1 = 15
n2 = 15

escalc(measure = "SMD",
       ti = t,
       n1i = n1,
       n2i = n2)

\[\begin{aligned}
&d=\frac{t}{\sqrt{n}} \\
&J= 1 - \frac{3}{4(n - 1) - 1} \\
&g=J*d\\
&Var(g) = \frac{1}{n} + \frac{g^2}{2(n - 1)} \\
\end{aligned}\]

title: Single-group effect sizes
text:
While most meta-analyses concern the relationships between two variables, often reflecting experimental treatments, sometimes we’re interested in summarizing single-group measurements and then analyzing these measurements in relation to moderators.
For example, imagine you want to understand the drivers of predator attacks on livestock. Various studies have reported predator diets or kill frequencies, allowing you to obtain the proportion of diet that contains livestock (Dhungana et al. 2026). These single-group proportions can be converted to effect sizes (so that they obtain a sampling variance estimation). You can then use metaregression to evaluate the influence of various moderators (e.g., human density, elevation, prey density) on predator depredation rates of livestock.

title: Single-group effect sizes
text:
Single group means
The single group standardized mean is the mean divided by standard deviation to create a unit-free index, similar to SMD. As such, this effect size can accept values ≤ 0.
In escalc:

escalc(measure = "SMN",
       mi = 10,
       sdi = 1.5,
       ni = 15)

This, like SMD, can be interpreted as the number of standard deviations the mean is from 0. Given that standard deviation influences the mean, this effect size may be less preferred with overdispersed data (as with SMD). See here, where we discuss how to diagnose overdispersion in your data.

title: Single-group effect sizes
text:
Log-transformed mean
The log-transformed mean is a single group corollary to lnRoM. This effect size cannot accept negative values. As with lnRoM, the point estimate for log-transformed mean is not influenced by standard deviation, which is instead accounted for by the sampling variance estimate.
In escalc:

escalc(measure = "MNLN",
       mi = 10,
       sdi = 1.5,
       ni = 15)

As such, this effect size is likely better suited for overdispersed data.

title: Continuous outcomes between two groups
text:
This class of effect sizes is among the most commonly used in ecology and evolution. These effect sizes compare a continuous response between two groups. For example:
Studies like these often report the same basic information: a mean, standard deviation, and sample size for each group. However, the same data can answer several different biological questions.
Before choosing an effect size, ask what kind of difference matters:
These effect sizes may use similar information and may be interpreted in similar ways, but they do not answer the same question. The biological question should determine which one you use.
In this chapter, we focus on SMD and lnRoM. These are important options for comparing mean responses of continuous variables between two groups.
In addition to SMD and lnRoM, comparisons of continuous responses between two groups can often be complimented by analyses of different effect sizes, which capture more than just mean differences. For example, lnM describes magnitude of differences regardless of direction and lnVR/lnCVR describe differences in variability between two groups. These require the same statistical ingredients as SMD and lnRoM. We discuss lnM here and lnCVR/lnVR here
Choosing between SMD and lnRoM is not trivial. The appropriate choice depends on the biological quantity you want to estimate and whether the data meet the assumptions of that effect size.

title: Continuous outcomes between two groups
text:
Standardized Mean Difference (SMD)
SMD is akin to a test statistic: it is the ratio of signal (the mean difference between two groups) and noise (the pooled standard deviation of those groups). You can see this in the point estimate formula for the definition formula of SMD (called Cohen’s d):
\[
\begin{aligned}
d = \frac{m_1 - m_2}{sd_{pooled}}
\end{aligned}
\] with \(sd_{pooled}\) defined as:
\[
sd_{pooled}= \sqrt{ \frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2+(n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2}}\\
\] The formula above, for \(d\), returns values between \(-\infty\) and \(\infty\). These values describe the number of pooled standard deviations between groups 1 and 2 and are generally interpreted with the following rules of thumb:

\(SMD \approx |0.2|\) is a weak effect
\(SMD \approx |0.5|\) is a moderate effect
\(SMD \approx |0.8|\) is a strong effect

For our running biological example, we can plug our values in and produce: \[
\begin{aligned}
sd_{pooled}=
\sqrt{\frac{19(3^2)+19(2^2)}{38}}
=\sqrt{6.5}
\approx 2.55\ \mathrm{g}.
\end{aligned}
\] And a Cohen’s d value of: \[
d=\frac{12-10}{2.55}\approx 0.78.
\] However, Cohen’s d is biased at low sample sizes. For that reason, we will also apply a small sample size correction factor (\(J\)) (Hedges 1981), to calculate a modified version of SMD called Hedges’ g. \(J\) approaches 1 as sample size increases, which means that with high sample sizes, Hedges’ g becomes indistinguishable from from Cohen’s d:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&df = n_1+n_2-2\\
&J \approx 1-\frac{3}{4df-1}\\
&g = Jd
\end{aligned}
\] As such, our final SMD value for our running biological example is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&df = 20+20-2
= 38\\
&J \approx 1-\frac{3}{4df-1} \approx 0.98\\
&g = Jd = 0.98 * 0.78 = 0.76
\end{aligned}
\] This value of 0.76 equates to a moderately strong effect: a change in 0.76 standard deviations between the control and treatment groups.
This can be done in R using metafor’s escalc function:

escalc(m1i = 12, sd1i = 3, n1i = 20,
       m2i = 10, sd2i = 2, n2i = 20,
       measure = "SMD")


      yi     vi 
1 0.7689 0.1074

title: Continuous outcomes between two groups
text:
Log-transformed ratio of means (lnRoM)
lnRoM is intended for measurements on a ratio scale, which means the group means must be positive and greater than zero. It is not suitable when the means have opposite signs, which may happen when dealing with before-after-control-impact experimental designs.
lnRoM tells a very different story than SMD. The point estimate only accounts for the group means—all signal and no noise. This can lead to very meta-analytic results. For example, if all of the studies in your dataset found non-significant differences between a control and experimental treatment, an SMD-based meta-analysis is likely to also find very weak differences between those groups.
However, an lnRoM-based meta-analysis may find strong and significant differences because the lnRoM point estimate only accounts for the mean, and not for variation. Instead, variability is captured by lnRoM’s sampling variance estimates—which influence the relative weight of each effect size in your models.
The point estimate definition formula for lnRoM makes it clear why:
\[
\begin{aligned}
lnRoM = \ln(\frac{m_1}{m_2})
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}\] As you can see, this formula does not account for variability. The point estimate simply describes the ratio of means, with the natural logarithm making this comparable around zero. A ratio of 1 becomes \(\ln(1)=0\); reciprocal ratios have equal magnitudes and opposite signs.
Using our example biological data: \[
\begin{aligned}
\ln(\frac{m_1}{m_2})=\ln(\frac{12}{10})=0.18
\end{aligned}
\]
The lnRoM point estimate of 0.18 can be interpreted by converting it back to % change. This means that if you’re fitting meta-analytic models on an lnRoM dataset, you can convert your overall model estimates to % change, which can dramatically improve your communication ability in plain language. This is one the great advantages of lnRoM.
To convert to percent change, you merely undo the natural logarithm, subtract 1 and multiply by 100. For our lnRoM point estimate of 0.18:
\[
100(e^{0.18} - 1) \approx 19.72\%.
\] This means that the treatment led to a 20% increase in plant biomass in our warming treatment.
In R, we can calculate lnRoM as follows:

escalc(m1i = 12, sd1i = 3, n1i = 20,
       m2i = 10, sd2i = 2, n2i = 20,
       measure = "ROM")


      yi     vi 
1 0.1829 0.0051 


And to convert to % change:

100 * (exp(0.18) - 1)

[1] 19.72174

title: Continuous outcomes between two groups
text:
The small-sample size correction
With SMD, we used \(J\) to correct for bias at low sample sizes. A similar second-order derived estimator exists for lnRoM to account for bias at low sample sizes (Lajeunesse 2015). This correction is important if your dataset has small sample sizes and is not overdispersed (which we’ll discuss further below).
This correction changes the lnRoM point estimate formula to:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ln\left(\frac{m_1}{m_2}\right)
+\frac{1}{2}
\left(
\frac{sd_1^2}{n_1m_1^2}
-\frac{sd_2^2}{n_2m_2^2}
\right).
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}\]
If your data is overdispersed, then this small sample size correction can become problematic, because the point estimate now incorporates standard deviation. In that case, you should use the uncorrected, first-order formula for lnRoM.
In escalc, you can do this by toggling the correct=TRUE (the default) to FALSE:

# Bias-corrected version, the default:
escalc(m1i = 12, sd1i = 3, n1i = 20,
       m2i = 10, sd2i = 2, n2i = 20,
       measure = "ROM")


      yi     vi 
1 0.1829 0.0051 

# Uncorrected:
escalc(m1i = 12, sd1i = 3, n1i = 20,
       m2i = 10, sd2i = 2, n2i = 20,
       measure = "ROM", correct = FALSE)


      yi     vi 
1 0.1823 0.0051 


Or in eff_size:

eff_size(x1 = 12, sd1 = 3, n1 = 20,
         x2 = 10, sd2 = 2, n2 = 20,
         effect_type = "lnRoM",
         default_formulas = FALSE)

lnRoM cannot accept x1 or x2 ≤ 0. 
 Leaving it to user's discretion to check prior to execution.

Using the formulas:
     yi_first <- log(x1 / x2)
     yi_second <- log(x1 / x2) + 0.5 * (sd1^2/(n1 * x1^2) - sd2^2/(n2 * x2^2))
     vi_first <- sd1^2 / (n1 * x1^2) + sd2^2 / (n2 * x2^2)
     vi_second <- sd1^2 / (n1 * x1^2) + sd2^2 / (n2 * x2^2) + 0.5 * ( (sd1^4 / (n1^2 * x1^4)) + (sd2^4 / (n2^2 * x2^4))) 
Be sure that all variables in formula are correctly named.


    yi_first yi_second vi_first   vi_second
       <num>     <num>    <num>       <num>
1: 0.1823216 0.1828841 0.005125 0.005131883


with _first and _second referring to uncorrected definition formula (Equation 4) and second-order (Equation 5) estimators respectively.

title: Continuous outcomes between two groups
text:
Values ≤ 0
A key consideration in choosing between SMD and lnRoM is whether your dataset has means ≤ 0. These may occur for a variety of reasons, including because of before-after-control-impact experimental designs or other data presentation formats. If means ≤ 0 are common in your dataset then you may have to use SMD simply in order to make use of all of your data.






ImportantData bounded between 0 and 1



Means±SD bounded between 0 and 1 are challenged by their numeric properties: variance tends to retreat to zero when the mean approaches 0 or 1 (Macartney et al. 2022).
To resolve this for SMD and lnRoM effect sizes, you need to transform both the means and the standard deviations, using an arcsin-square root transformation on the mean and an equation derived using the delta method to standardize the standard deviation (see Macartney et al. (2022)).
We cover this transformation in our extraction challenges page here

title: Continuous outcomes between two groups
text:
Dimensionality
Both SMD and lnRoM are standardized, which allow us to compare results across studies even if their units were different. However, what if one study measured a response in meters but another study measured it in area (\(meter^2\)) and a third study measured the same response in volume (\(meter^3\))?
Imagine vegetation studies or morphological measurements of an organism or the size of a tumor. Depending on the effect size you choose, the results can be strongly affected by these added dimensions—which is an overlooked problem in meta-analysis.
For lnRoM, this is a very serious problem—the estimated effect at dimension 1 will double at the second dimension!
Let us demonstrate. We’ll create a starting dataset at one dimension and then we’ll increase the dimensions from 1 to 2 and 3, by recreating the underlying distribution, recalculating our summary statistics, and calculating SMD or lnRoM effect sizes. Feel free to unfold the code to see how we did this:

# Simulate data for two groups
sim1 <- rnorm(n = 1e8, mean = 15, sd = .6)
sim2 <- rnorm(n = 1e8, mean = 13, sd = .7)

# First dimension:
dim1.1 <- sim1
dim1.2 <- sim2

# Second dimension simulated data for groups 1 and 2
dim2.1 <- sim1^2
dim2.2 <- sim2^2

# Third dimension simulated data for groups 1 and 2
dim3.1 <- sim1^3
dim3.2 <- sim2^3

# Create a data.table of the summary statistics:
dat <- data.frame(m1 = c(mean(dim1.1), mean(dim2.1), mean(dim3.1)),
                  m2 = c(mean(dim1.2), mean(dim2.2), mean(dim3.2)),
                  sd1 = c(sd(dim1.1), sd(dim2.1), sd(dim3.1)),
                  sd2 = c(sd(dim1.2), sd(dim2.2), sd(dim3.2)),
                  n1 = 50,
                  n2 = 50,
                  dimensions = c(1, 2, 3))

dat <- escalc(measure = "ROM",
              m1i = m1, m2i = m2,
              sd1i = sd1, sd2i = sd2,
              n1i = n1, n2i = n2,
              data = dat,
              var.names = c("yi_rom", "vi_rom"))

dat <- escalc(measure = "SMD",
              m1i = m1, m2i = m2,
              sd1i = sd1, sd2i = sd2,
              n1i = n1, n2i = n2,
              data = dat,
              var.names = c("yi_smd", "vi_smd")) |> 
  setDT()
# dat

# Convert ROM to % change:
dat <- dat %>%
  mutate(percent_change = (exp(yi_rom) - 1) * 100)
#
p1 <- ggplot(data = dat, 
       aes(x = dimensions, y = yi_rom))+
  geom_path()+
  geom_point(size = 4)+
  ylab("lnRoM point estimate")+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 2, 3))+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none")

p2 <- ggplot(data = dat, 
       aes(x = dimensions, y = percent_change))+
  geom_path()+
  geom_point(size = 4)+
  ylab("Estimated % change")+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 2, 3))+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none")

p1 / p2







As you can see, the lnRoM effect size doubled and then tripled as the dimensions increased. In ecology and evolutionary biology, which commonly pool measurements at different dimensions, this is obviously a huge problem!
Now let’s look at SMD. Since the y axis values are not comparable, we’ll plot the raw SMD as well as the difference of each dimension to the first dimension, to indicate how large of an effect dimensionality had on the strength of the SMD estimate in reference to our rules of thumb








SMD is still somewhat affected by the change in dimensions but to a far lesser extent.
For this reason, we suggest that if you are committed to using an lnRoM effect size, that you must record the number of dimensions of each measurement. You can use these to divide the resulting effect size point estimate by the number of dimensions to standardize dimensionality. E.g., if the measurement was across 2 dimensions (\(m^2\)) then divide by 2 and if across 3 dimensions (\(m^3\)), divide by 3.
However, there may be many cases where the number of dimensions of the measurement may be unclear.






Important



The dimensionality problem of lnRoM is quite perilous given that lnRoM is the dominant effect size used in ecology and evolution. It may be that the majority of ecological meta-analyses, especially vegetation meta-analyses, need to be redone.

title: Continuous outcomes between two groups
text:
Overdispersion
SMD and lnRoM assume that the underlying data generation process is normal. This assumption can be broken if the data is overdispersed—which is remarkably common in ecology and evolution, especially with abundance or count data. This can lead to biased point and sampling variance estimates.
Overdispersion affects these effect sizes differently. For SMD, they directly affect the point estimate, because the point estimate is a ratio of signal to noise. Overdispersed data will tend to make SMDs approach 0. For lnRoM, the point estimate is robust to overdispersion (as long as you use the uncorrected definition formula). However, the sampling variance estimate is sensitive to overdispersion.
There are as yet no effect sizes formulated for overdispersed data. As such, if there is overdispersed data in your dataset, you should:

Exclude effect sizes that are overdispersed as a sensitivity analysis in comparison to your full dataset
Use the inverse of effective sample size as your meta-analytic weight, instead of sampling variance, as an additional sensitivity analysis.

As you’ll see throughout this tutorial, sensitivity tests are the annoying reality of meta-analysis.
Testing for overdispersion should be part of your analytic workflow. The easiest way to test for overdispersion is to calculate the coefficient of variation (\(CV\)) for your control and treatment groups. \(CV\) is the ratio of standard deviation to the mean (\(sd/x\)).
We consider a \(CV>2\) to be indicative of overdispersion. However, for lnRoM, Lajeunesse (2015) suggested a small sample-size corrected threshold based on the standardized mean, derived from the Geary test Hedges et al. (1999). Let \(m\) be the group mean, \(sd\) be the standard deviation and \(n\) be your group sample size:
\[
\begin{aligned}
G' = \frac{m}{sd}*\frac{4*n^{3/2}}{1+4*n}
\end{aligned}
\tag{6}\]
There are several suggested thresholds for this value that can be used to exclude potentially overdispersed and problematic data. Lajuennesse suggested excluding values ≥3 for lnRoM.
If a lot of your data is overdispersed, one option is to compare the bias-corrected and uncorrected lnRoM estimators as a sensitivity analysis. In current versions of metafor, request the uncorrected estimator with correct = FALSE; it is not the default. We also recommend conducting sensitivity analyses that exclude data identified as potentially problematic using clearly specified criteria, and comparing sampling-variance weights with effective-sample-size weights when justified (Nakagawa et al. 2023).
HOW DOES THIS APPLY DIFFERENTLY TO SMD VS LNROM???

Click to see a demonstration of overdispersion
Let’s do this in R with a \(CV>2\) threshold and the Geary-Lajuennesse threshold of 3, using a dataset provided by the metafor package:

data("dat.gibson2002")
dat <- dat.gibson2002

# Drop NA values for the SMD type effect sizes
dat <- dat %>% filter(!is.na(m1i))

# Calculate coefficient of variation:
dat <- dat %>%
  mutate(cv1 = sd1i / m1i,
         cv2 = sd2i / m2i)

n_overdispersed <- dat %>% 
  filter(cv1 > 2 | cv2 > 2) %>%
  nrow()
n_overdispersed/nrow(dat) * 100

[1] 61.53846


It looks like 46% of this dataset has a \(CV>2\)!

# With the Geary-Lajuennesse threshold:
geary <- function(sd, m, n){
  (m/sd) * (4*n^(3/2))/(1 + 4*n)
}

dat <- dat %>%
  mutate(gl1 = geary(sd = sd1i, m = m1i, n = n1i),
         gl2 = geary(sd = sd2i, m = m2i, n = n2i))


n_failed_geary <- dat %>%
  filter(gl1 < 3 | gl2 < 3) %>%
  nrow()
n_failed_geary/nrow(dat) * 100

[1] 38.46154


Values of 3 or greater pass the improved Geary test. The code above reports the percentage of effect sizes for which either group has a value below 3 and therefore fails the test. If many effect sizes fail, compare the full analysis with an analysis that excludes the flagged values.
An alternative approach is to use the inverse of effective sample size as your meta-analytic model weight, instead of sampling variance. This may be essential when a significant amount of your data is overdispersed. This is a method that produces reasonable meta-analytic estimates, despite ignoring standard deviation (Nakagawa et al. 2023).
Effective sample size is defined as: \[
\begin{aligned}
N_{0} = \frac{4n_1n_2}{n_1 + n_2}\\
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}\]
Let’s go through a full example, with lnRoM as our effect size.
First we’ll calculate lnRoM point estimates and sampling variance:

dat <- escalc(measure = "ROM", 
              m1i = m1i, m2i = m2i, 
              sd1i = sd1i, sd2i = sd2i,
              n1i = n1i, n2i = n2i,
              data = dat, append = TRUE) |> 
  setDT()

Now, let’s run a model excluding the overdispersed data:
